#3756. Marilyn Monroe and Arthur Miller’s Tragic Love Story

“I think you’re the saddest girl I ever met.”

“You’re the first man that ever said that. I’m usually told how happy I am.”

This exchange, from The Misfits, written by Arthur Miller, shows Marilyn Monroe drawing closer to something other than the “dumb blonde” persona for which Hollywood praised her.

After all, the actor—who was born in Los Angeles in 1926 and died in the City of Angels in 1962 at the age of 36—wanted to be taken seriously as a performer. She never fully identified with the image Hollywood created for her. She spent her limited free time enjoying uncharacteristic pastimes, as evidenced by one of her most famous photographs, which depicts her reading James Joyce’s Ulysses while donning a striped tank top, black shorts, and a deep, melancholic gaze.

Marilyn Monroe reads a book in her room at the Hotel Ambassador in midtown Manhattan, March 1955.

“A sex symbol becomes a thing. I just hate to be a thing,” said Monroe to Life magazine in 1962, reflecting on her strained relationship with Hollywood.

Miller, who was born in New York in 1915 and passed away in 2005, initially believed he would be a good partner for Monroe, whose life was marked by great successes, but also abandonment and her unfortunate inability to have children—one of the most painful issues for Monroe.

Monroe and Miller first met in 1950, when he was in Los Angeles with director Elia Kazan. It was Kazan who introduced them.

Monroe and Miller began talking, and he emphasized her potential to become a dramatic actor on New York stages. He struck a chord.

In the mid-1950s, the star left Hollywood and moved to New York to study, attending The Actors Studio and working with Lee Strasberg. She met with Miller again in the Big Apple, and in 1955, they began dating seriously, joining two seemingly distant worlds.

Marilyn Monroe and playwright Arthur Miller play with his dog Hugo,at Miller’s summer home on June 25, 1956.

Monroe felt respected by him, unlike the way she felt in Hollywood, which she once called “an overcrowded brothel, a merry-go-round with beds for horses,” in her unfinished memoir, My Story.

Miller, who had won the Pulitzer Prize in 1949 for Death of a Salesman, was captivated by her and ended his failing marriage.

The subsequent marriage between Monroe and Miller—her third marriage, his second—took place on June 29, 1956, in White Plains, New York. A few days later, a private Jewish ceremony was also held, following the actor’s conversion to Judaism.

The first major rift in their marriage stemmed from ongoing tension between public and private life. Miller wanted a more secluded, domestic life; Monroe wanted a family, but she was not willing to give up the career she had so painstakingly built.

For the 1957 film The Prince and the Showgirl—directed by and starring Laurence Olivier, with Monroe as the female lead and coproducer—the actor and her husband moved to England, where tensions rose.

Arthur Miller and Marilyn Monroe after their wedding.

Monroe found some of Miller’s notes, in which he expressed disappointment with their marriage and admitted to sometimes feeling embarrassed around his friends in the cultural world.

It was one of the hardest moments in their relationship: Monroe discovered that the man who seemed to recognize her talent and intelligence also viewed her through the very same lens from which she was trying to free herself.

In her own notebooks, she reflected on her fear of becoming “someone’s wife” and losing her independence.

Miller would later say that he wrote very little during the years of his marriage.

Monroe, meanwhile, was struggling to become a mother. During her marriage, she experienced a miscarriage, an ectopic pregnancy, and another spontaneous termination of pregnancy.

On the set of The Prince and the Showgirl, her difficulties increased: She often arrived late, struggled to work consistently, and her relationship with Laurence Olivier became strained.

In the background, Miller faced a trial, as he had refused to name Communist Party members and sympathizers. He was convicted of contempt of Congress in 1957, but the conviction was overturned the following year.

Marilyn Monroe and her former husband Arthur Miller as they leave Doctors Hospital on August 10, 1957, after she recovered from a 10-day hospital stay following an ectopic pregnancy.

Despite Monroe publicly expressing her support for her husband, the cracks in their marriage turned into chasms. Arguments, a lack of trust, disillusionment, drugs, alcohol, all of it became too difficult to contain.

The point of no return was another feature film, The Misfits, written by Miller for Monroe.

The desert setting where it was filmed didn’t help. Amid hellish temperatures, Monroe and Miller were no longer on speaking terms, even though they were staying at the same hotel. Intermediaries were needed just to get them to communicate.

It was during this shoot that Miller met the photographer Inge Morath, whom he would later marry in February 1962.

They divorced shortly after The Misfits was released in theaters.

After The Misfits, Monroe went through one of the most difficult periods of her life. In 1961 she was admitted to the Payne Whitney Psychiatric Clinic in New York. Joe DiMaggio intervened to have her transferred to another facility.

Marilyn Monroe’s photo shoot at Hollywood agent Johnny Hyde’s backyard in Beverly Hills, California, 1957.

Before her death, Monroe nevertheless continued to work, seek roles, and imagine a life different from the one others intended for her.

In a 1988 interview that aired on the Italian network Rai, journalist and writer Enzo Biagi asked Miller: “How do you want to remember Marilyn Monroe?”

He replied: “She made everyone believe she was very happy, but I didn’t believe it. She was very depressed, but she had the extraordinary talent of being able to mask her state of mind. She wore a mask because she was suffering too much. She was completely unable to cope with her depression, but she had been an abused child. She was looking for someone to save her.”

Originally published by Vanity Fair Italia.

#3755. Ubisoft and at least two other companies are interested in buying Arkane, according to new report

Arkane Studios, which spent the last several months in limbo following Xbox's decision to divest itself from the studio, has apparently received buyout offers from several bidders.

Arkane was recently given until December to find a buyer and avoid closure, an extension from the previous November deadline, thanks to union efforts. Now, according to a Bloomberg report, a few companies have offered to buy Arkane from Microsoft.

The report names French publisher Ubisoft among at least three companies currently in talks with Microsoft to acquire the French studio. No decision has been made, however. The report also said Xbox considered selling Arkane to its management.

Should any of these offers be accepted, it would mean saving Arkane from closure, potentially saving up to 217 jobs and allowing the team to finish Marvel's Blade, which recent reports suggested is nearing completion. Bloomberg, however, said the game is "expected to be released within the next year or two", so it may not be as close as we think.

Arkane is one of several studios Xbox divested itself from as part of CEO Asha Sharma's big plan to reset the business, which saw over 1,600 job cuts with a further 1,600 to be made by the end of the fiscal year.

Studio divestitures include Psychonauts studio Double Fine, South of Midnight studio Compulsion Games, and State of Decay studio Undead Labs - which have all managed to go independent. Hellblade developer Ninja Theory and Arkane had the biggest question marks hanging over them, with Ninja Theory's fate seemingly the most dire after failing to find a buyer.

Given the December deadline Arkane was granted, we're likely to learn the identity of the studio's new owner in the near future.

#3754. Spencer Pratt Defends Staying in $1,200-a-Night Hotel During L.A. Mayor Race

Spencer Pratt is setting the record straight about why he stayed at a luxury hotel during his campaign to become Los Angeles’ next mayor.

“Remember when you first met me? For those of you in the [Pacific] Palisades, that was likely many years ago, but the majority of folks met me when my first campaign ad dropped back in April,” Pratt, 43, wrote via X on Tuesday, November 3. “I showed Karen Bass’ and Nithya Raman’s multimillion-dollar homes and then showed everybody the grim reality of what became of my home. A sleek, Airstream perched precariously on my hillside lot, a stark contrast to the nuked out wreckage where my home used to be.”

After Pratt and his wife, Heidi Montag, lost their home in the January 2025 Palisades fire, The Hills alum worked to get an Airstream trailer installed at his burned property.

While running to become Los Angeles’ next mayor, however, Pratt found himself in controversy when outlets claimed he was actually staying at the Hotel Bel-Air, which has a nightly rate between $900 to $1,200 for standard luxury rooms.

“When the media found out I was staying there, they were most certainly not cozy nor at ease. The backlash was intense, and predictably so,” Pratt shared via X. “Now, in many ways, our campaign was perfectly fine with the controversy, because the kerfuffle over me staying at a hotel just reminded everyone of my opponent’s biggest failure; Karen Bass is the reason I didn’t have a home to go to. But, nonetheless, it was becoming such a big controversy, it was eating up all the oxygen in the room, and it was a distraction from all my winning policy ideas; instead of talking about the campaign, we were talking about a damn hotel.”

Pratt consistently criticized Bass, 73, for not being present in Los Angeles at the time of the Palisades fire. He also claimed she was not prepared to deal with a fire that destroyed more than 6,800 structures. (Bass and Los Angeles City Council member Nithya Raman ultimately received the most votes in the June primary, leaving Pratt off the ballot for Tuesday’s election.)

In his X post, Pratt answered the question some may be asking about his pricey accommodations.

“Why is he spending $1,200 a night? Why couldn’t he stay somewhere for $300 a night? Well, the answer to that question is not as pretty as any of us may like to hear,” he said. “Most people simply presumed that I was being a bougie spoiled brat, and that I was abusing campaign funds. … At the time, I couldn’t explain the math to people, and my campaign staff told me I wasn’t allowed to divulge the real reason I had to stay there, but now that the election is coming to a close, I don’t need to listen to anyone anymore.”

According to Pratt, he endured “numerous death threats” to the point where he had to hire full-time security.

He described the Hotel Bel-Air as a “unique” property “surrounded with a fortress wall.”

“Unlike normal hotels, it is a very secure facility, which is why Presidents and Royalty like the Prince of Wales or Saint Thomas of Cruise feel comfortable staying there,” he explained. “When my security team dropped me off behind the walls of the Bel Air, they felt good about leaving me alone in the secure facility. Had I stayed anywhere else, I would have needed to book out 3 rooms for my team to maintain overnight security, which would’ve cost an additional $3,000 per night. Paradoxically, by this calculation, I was actually saving a ton of money by staying at the secure Bel Air; even staying at a Motel 6 would’ve cost me more money, and in a campaign…money is everything.”

Pratt said he appreciated having security “watching everything and everyone around me.”

“Now that there’s no campaign, I can’t afford that level of protection, even though I still deal with death threats and trespassers at my property, routinely,” the Guy You Loved to Hate: Confessions from a Reality TV Villain author claimed before promoting an app called Patrol.

Pratt continued, “This is the way of the future, and I’m doing everything in my power to keep my family safe. … I’m done leaving our lives in the hands of government. We are on our own.”

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

At this point, I've accepted that Taylor Swift operates on an entirely different creative clock than the rest of us. Of all the behind-the-scenes stories to come out of the 2026 movie schedule, I wasn't prepared for what Toy Story 5 director Andrew Stanton had to say about how quickly she wrote "I Knew It, I Knew You" after seeing the Pixar sequel. The guy has spent decades making some of animation's most beloved films, but apparently even he couldn't keep his language family-friendly when he heard what she'd done. Here’s his NOT PG reaction after Swift wrote the song in less than a day.

During a recent Q&A with Swift, Stanton recalled how the singer ended up contributing a song to the film. Swift's brother Austin had urged her to watch an early cut while she was exhausted from the Eras Tour, and she finally agreed once she'd recovered. She immediately connected with Jessie, the cowgirl at the center of the sequel, and called Stanton from the screening room that afternoon. Hours later, Disney's music team called him again, this time with news he couldn't quite believe:

You [Swift] saw it that morning with your brother, and that was at 10 o'clock. And then at noon my FaceTime rings, and it's from Tom, but it's you guys, you and Austin, and you're still in your seats and you're gushing about the movie. And you said, ‘You want to do the song?’ Like, there wasn't even a debate about this or a discussion. It was just, ‘You want to do the song?’ We're like, ‘Great, great, great.’ And we almost got off so that you couldn't change your mind.

I love that Stanton's first instinct was to end the call before the “Shake it Off” performer could reconsider. Getting her to agree to write the song was already a pretty big deal, but he had no idea just how quickly things were about to move. He continued:

And then I go home that night, and Tom calls me, the head of music, and says, ‘She wrote the song.’ I'm like, ‘What?’ And I'm like, ‘No, no, no, no. She found it or she had it already. She relabeled it.’ And he's like, ‘No, she's in the studio and she's written the song, and I'm driving right now to hear it.’ I'm like, ‘Wow, get the f out of here.’

I kind of love that his first assumption was that Swift must have quietly pulled an old song off the shelf and given it a Toy Story label. He seemed genuinely baffled that someone could watch a movie in the morning and have a song ready before dinner. Apparently Stanton wasn't the only Toy Story veteran surprised by the music icon's involvement.

Stanton's day somehow got weirder. Around 9 that evening, he got another FaceTime call, this time from Disney CEO Bob Iger, who stood beside Swift and raved about the track. Stanton recalled asking the music A-lister if she'd really written it before calling her "a beast." The director didn't hear the finished song in person until several days later, when he flew to Los Angeles. He added:

I got choked up when I heard it. And the only other time I've heard a song that just dropped from thin air and was perfect was when Randy Newman came in and played 'You've Got a Friend in Me" on a piano with six of us.

That's serious praise, especially coming from someone who helped shape Pixar's original era. Newman's "You've Got a Friend in Me" remains one of the most recognizable movie songs of all time, and Swift has said she didn't want her contribution to feel out of place. She wrote and produced "I Knew It, I Knew You" with longtime collaborator Jack Antonoff, drawing on her country roots and Jessie's complicated history of being left behind.

While the song came together ridiculously fast, Stanton offered a beautiful explanation: Swift's lifelong connection to Toy Story prepared her for it. The filmmaker said the tune really took "a lifetime" to write, starting with her watching the films as a kid. I think that's a much sweeter explanation than the one he gave on that first phone call.

Toy Story 5 is now streaming with a Disney+ subscription, with the Taylor Swift and Antonoff track playing over the end credits. And if you need a reason to revisit the flick, picture Stanton losing his mind and dropping F-bombs on FaceTime over the song.

Ryan graduated from Missouri State University with a BA in English/Creative Writing. An expert in all things horror, Ryan enjoys covering a wide variety of topics. He's also a lifelong comic book fan and an avid watcher of Game of Thrones and House of the Dragon.

#3751. Guild Wars gets its first major gameplay update in almost 20 years

ArenaNet and co-dev studio 2Weeks have announced Guild Wars Afterlife - the first major update for the game in nearly 20 years.

Coming to PC and mobile, Afterlife will add a new dynamic dungeon that'll morph after each run, and a skill-drafting system that'll allow you to create a distinct skill bar that'll change each time you take it on. There'll also of course be a new narrative to dig into, as players find new characters to interact with, and the new region of Xotecha to explore.

Afterlife is set to release on the 13th January next year, and will retail for $29.99 / €29.99 / £25.99. However, if you pre-order it between now and the 13th January, you can get it at a 20 percent discount.

This is a pretty big deal: the last time Guild Wars 1 got a massive injection of new stuff to dive into was back in August 2007 with the Eye of the North expansion. Following this, ArenaNet would move on to focus on Guild Wars 2 for the most part, leaving Guild Wars 1 servers up and running during that time.

However, the game has itself entered something of an afterlife following almost two decades of inaction. ArenaNet released Guild Wars Reforged - an enhanced upgrade to the original MMO - late last year. It also received a new dungeon in April, which has enticed new and returning players to dive back in.

Afterlife's reveal comes as ArenaNet is juggling development on three live service games at once. You've got Guild Wars Reforged (with Afterlife) of course, the more traditional MMORPG Guild Wars 2, and the highly-anticipated action-oriented Guild Wars 3. All will receive updates and support simultaneously, a sign of confidence in the health of the MMO space.

"See that mountain? You can overanalyze it."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When the Greybeards invite you to High Hrothgar in Skyrim, you have to climb a mountain to reach them. There's a messenger called Klimmek waiting in the village of Ivarstead at the bottom to warn you what an arduous journey this is going to be. To get to the top of the Throat of the World, he says, you have to work your way up The 7,000 Steps.

It's well-documented that there aren't actually 7,000 steps carved into the side of the mountain. Some of them are buried under the snow, making an exact count impossible, but the actual number is closer to 700. And even if you argue that The 7,000 Steps refers to the number of footsteps it takes to ascend the mountain, according to the dedicated researchers at the Ultimate Elder Scrolls Portal it only takes "approximately 2,400 footsteps" to get there.

As part of Bethesda's 40th anniversary, which included the reveal of The Elder Scrolls 6's subtitle, the studio reminisced about their previous work, which is how we know they really did try to get 7,000 steps into the side of the mountain.

While not responsible for the rough layout of Skyrim's terrain, I was responsible for refining the shapes of High Hrothgar. I would look at the mountain from various viewpoints and tried to keep the shape interesting. My work on the "Throat of the World" was not limited to sculpting the mountain, but also included cluttering and dressing the mountain with visual effects, plants, and objects. This of course, included the infamous 7,000 steps. Now, I love trying to be as faithful to lore or real-life as possible and I did my darndest to find a way to fit all 7,000 steps into the storied path. However, my best attempt to do so included extending far past Ivartstead, wrapping around the mountain and ending near Whiterun in the frozen tundra. It turns out, 7,000 is quite a lot! By the way, my work did NOT include enemy encounters, so I take no responsibility for the Frost Troll that was the woe of many players.

Of course, like most open world games, Skyrim isn't designed to scale—otherwise the capital city of Solitude would have a population of less than 100 people. But in the same way that for every named NPC we should assume there are a bunch of people off-camera, distances are compressed so that it doesn't take a week to get anywhere. For every step we watched the Dragonborn climb there are another nine implied steps we don't see, and even more frost trolls.

#3749. Model Sahara Ray's Death Certificate Reveals New Details: Report

The death certificate for Sahara Ray has reportedly revealed new details about where the model died and more.

Ray’s remains are set to be cremated on November 10, with her mother’s Los Angeles home listed as the place of final disposition, according to the certificate obtained by TMZ on Tuesday, November 3.

The certificate also confirmed that Sahara died at age 34 on October 18 at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles. Her cause of death remains deferred.

Ray’s family previously announced her death in a statement on October 19.

“She passed away last night surrounded by family at the hospital,” the family told TMZ. “She was so loved.”

Sahara, the daughter of Australian pro surfer Tony Ray, was born in Australia and grew up in California. She gained fame through her modeling career and developed a large following on social media. She also launched a swimwear line called Sahara Ray Swim.

Sahara made headlines in 2016 when she was spotted vacationing with Justin Bieber in Hawaii. She has also reportedly been linked to singer and future Traitors star Cody Simpson.

In 2024, Sahara revealed she was diagnosed with Guillain-Barré syndrome, a rare neurological disorder in which the body’s immune system attacks the nerves and causes weakness, numbness or paralysis.

“My whole life changed in an instant,” she wrote via Instagram at the time. “So thankful for my family and doctors for helping me get stronger everyday. Attitude is everything.”

In a video, she added, “Right now, I’m paralyzed from the tops of my upper thighs all the way down to my feet. I can’t walk at all.”

Sahara’s condition improved over time, and she announced in August 2025 that she was expecting her first baby. She welcomed a daughter named Snow in January.

Sahara’s sister, Ruby Ray, paid tribute to the content creator via social media after her death.

“My beautiful big sister, Sahara,” Ruby wrote on October 19 alongside several throwback photos with Sahara. “The most vivacious, intelligent, hilarious, kind, empathetic and breathtakingly beautiful soul. A force of nature. A light so bright that this world feels impossibly dimmer without her in it.”

She continued, “Sahara has moved from this life into another, and I am left trying to comprehend how someone so full of life can no longer be here to live it.”

Ruby called her older sister “everything extraordinary about being human” and “the most incredible person to ever walk this earth.”

“How cruel it is to love someone so deeply and have nowhere for that love to go. To have a lifetime of memories behind you, but no more tomorrows together,” she continued. “I don’t think there are words in any language capable of holding the weight of this heartbreak. I don’t know how to make sense of a world that keeps turning when mine feels as though it has stopped. … I just want my big sister.”

#3748. Dragon's Dogma 2 gets a timed collaboration with beloved anime and manga series Delicious in Dungeon, and it's out right now on PC, PlayStation and Xbox

Have you ever seen - or read - the wonderful Dungeon Meshi (known in English as 'Delicious in Dungeon')? It's a phenomenal manga series written and illustrated by Ryoko Kui, which was adapted into an anime series produced by Trigger in 2024. Long story short, it's about a group of adventurers in a fantasy world who lose an encounter with a dragon - who eats one of the party. What follows is a quest to revive the fallen party member (who happens to be the sister of one of the main characters), with the adventuring party learning to cook and eat monsters in dungeons as they uncover the stranger truth behind the world they inhabit.

If you can't tell, I think it's excellent, and the wait for the next season - landing in October 2027 - is practically killing me. It combines two of my biggest loves, cooking and fantasy, in a melting pot of a world that is intricately crafted and a story that is well-told. So imagine my surprise when I saw that Capcom announced a Dragon's Dogma 2: Dark Arisen x Delicious in Dungeon collaboration… and that it is live literally right now on PS5, Xbox, and PC platforms, coming in with a new update to the game.

"New allies and equipment are coming to the world of Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen with the arrival of Official Pawns and special collaboration outfits inspired by Delicious in Dungeon characters Laios and Marcille," reads a press release from the publisher. "Delicious in Dungeon is a hit manga series created by Ryoko Kui that follows the adventurer Laios and his party as they venture deep into a dungeon, cooking and eating the monsters they encounter along the way. These iconic characters collide with the classic fantasy world of Dragon's Dogma 2: Dark Arisen in a limited-time collaboration that arrives today for PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X|S, and PC."

For those playing on the newly-released Nintendo Switch 2 version of the game, this update will become available on Wednesday, 11th November.

Official Pawns modeled after the heavily-armored Laios and the elven mage Marcille can be recruited from the Riftstones, but there's a catch: these Pawns will only be available until Thursday, 28th January, 2027 on all platforms. So we've got a few months to play with them, but these helpful characters will not be permanent.

Additionally, players that load their data for Dragon's Dogma 2 during the collaboration period will receive special crossover outfits modeled after the attire of Laios and Marcille. These collaboration outfits will automatically be added to in-game storage and can be equipped by both the Arisen and Pawns. Once redeemed, these outfits will remain available even after the collaboration event ends.

Warning! The following contains spoilers for the Dexter: Resurrection episode "Risky Business." Stream the episode with a Paramount+ subscription, and read at your own risk!

Dexter Morgan is back on the prowl in the Season 2 premiere of Dexter: Resurrection, and I saw my favorite character again from last season! Eric Stonestreet returned once again as the Rapunzel Killer, but unfortunately, the return was short-lived.

Al Walker was tracked down by Dexter while on vacation with his family, as he was "working" while traveling to parks with his wife and kids. Dex was able to "do what he does," as Harrison puts it, and now no pony-tailed women have to worry about Rapunzel anymore. As satisfying as it was, I'm upset that Dexter: Resurrection is once again killing off fun guest stars.

Last season, Dexter: Resurrection gave us a great plot twist with the Serial Killers Club, which was quickly decimated by the Bay Harbor Butcher. There was a stacked cast of great guest stars, but by the end of the season, they were all dead except for Eric Stonestreet's character.

I had high hopes he'd be a big bad in Season 2, but that hope was squashed pretty quickly. I kind of guessed that would be the case given how many new guest stars were a part of this season, but it's disappointing the show didn't hold off and do a season dedicated to Rapunzel where Dex was on the road.

Dexter: Resurrection has two major guest stars this season, with Dan Stevens playing the Five Boroughs Killer and Brian Cox playing the New York Ripper. Both are big names tied to the Season 2 plot, and with Dexter being so concerned about legacy, it feels as though he's going to try to take out both of them.

I Have A Theory About Dexter: Resurrection And His Downfall. Why I Think Season 2 Could Address It

That's kind of the point of Dexter, to be fair. He's a serial killer who hunts other killers, so I can't sit here and act like Resurrection is going against what this series is about. I just feel as though he's felt very untouchable thus far, and maybe that these serial killers aren't as crafty as the ones from the original series?

I guess I fear that Dexter is becoming an Avengers-level type of anti-hero, and it feels like we haven't seen him face any real adversity. I know that's funny to say with him having been shot by his own son, but he and Harrison were able to put that aside really quickly. I'm just hoping we see Dex face a little more adversity in these upcoming episodes on the 2026 TV schedule, because I fear he's untouchable.

Catch new episodes of Dexter: Resurrection on Paramount+ on Fridays. I'm eager to see how the rest of this season plays out, and if Dexter and Harrison end the season in some trouble with the law.

#3746. Is This the Last Dance for Spain’s Prime Minister, Pedro Sánchez?

On September 23, Maricarmen Abascal, a partially disabled 87-year-old woman, was evicted from the apartment she rented in Madrid, where she had lived her entire life. Suffering from exhaustion caused by the long struggle to keep her home and then her subsequent eviction, she was admitted to a hospital. That same day, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez addressed the United Nations General Assembly in New York, an international forum where he has often promoted his foreign policy agenda, beginning with his first visit in 2018, when the politician who had been given the nickname Mr. Handsome met many of his counterparts around the globe. While Abascal would never return to her home (she died on October 7), and her eviction sparked widespread public outrage, Sánchez spoke of reforming international organizations, criticized the United States and Israel, and called for reining in the “tech oligarchs” at the helm of social media platforms and artificial intelligence companies: “The future of our sons and daughters must take precedence over the financial interests of these techno-oligarchs.”

No one in Spain paid attention to the speech: Abascal’s eviction sparked social unrest in a country that boasts of being the fastest-growing in Europe in terms of GDP, a fact on which the Banco de España and the International Monetary Fund agree. This has positioned the country as one of the leading economies in the eurozone, with unemployment having fallen to historic lows, according to official figures. In macroeconomic terms, the country has consistently appealed to international investors during Sánchez’s eight years in office, with foreign investment having grown 34% since 2018, according to calculations by the Ministry of Economy. It’s possible that the Spanish economy is experiencing its best period of growth since the country’s return to democracy in the mid-1970s. However, inflation, housing affordability, and low wages—the minimum wage has risen from 735 euros to 1,221 euros, but has failed to boost salaries broadly—are taking a toll on this economic boom.

And, among voters, there’s a sense of mismanagement during this legislative term. There was the migration crisis in Ceuta, a Spanish enclave on the North African coast that saw the sudden arrival of more than 72,000 migrants in late July. (Ceuta has just over 83,000 residents.) The crisis was not enough to get Sánchez to cut short his vacation. It revealed clashes between the ministers of defense and the interior, and it has taken nearly three months for the situation to be brought fully under control. Political scientist and university professor Lluís Orriols noted in El Periódico that the government had come out “badly” in its handling of crises such as the one in Ceuta and the eviction of Abascal—problems compounded by “legislative paralysis” (the government has managed to pass fewer than 40 laws in this legislative session, down from more than 100 in the previous one) and “corruption.” He asserted that only the strength of the economy had prevented “a government in shambles.”

After elections in 2023, Sánchez managed to secure another term, but without a clear left-wing majority, he had to rely on the support of several right or center-right nationalist parties without a legislative pact, which led to numerous parliamentary defeats. The coalition has failed to provide Spain with an effective government. The international landscape has not been particularly favorable either. Sánchez has gradually lost his key allies: That group of young, charismatic left-wing leaders who seemed to set the global agenda and had a special rapport with the Spanish leader have long since left power—the photos showing the admiration for Sánchez from Sanna Marin of Finland, Justin Trudeau of Canada, and Jacinda Ardern of New Zealand are now a thing of the past. His rapport with other European leaders such as Emmanuel Macron, a relationship marked by effusive camaraderie since way back in 2018, is of little use now that France is in turmoil and advocates for a return to austerity are gaining power in Europe. Even his relationship with Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission and one of Sánchez’s main supporters in the European Union, despite their ideological differences, is now of little relevance.

To top it all off, the prime minister came under fire even at Harvard, where he went shortly after his speech at the General Assembly to discuss AI, only to face sharp questions about Spanish politics and corruption. Even his safe role as a statesman was being eroded by political reality. Upon returning from his trip, an attempt to pass legislation that would prevent future situations like Abascal’s (in 2025 alone, there were more than 25,000 evictions, according to data from the General Council of the Judiciary) ran into obstacles in Spain’s fragmented parliament, which rejected every measure, and the legislative session came to a close. Meanwhile, the streets of Madrid and other cities began to fill with tents as people camped out in protest in a country where housing prices are rising by more than 10% annually, well above inflation and more so than wages. Whether it’s a matter of buying (nearly three out of every four Spaniards live in an owner-occupied home) or renting, both the Ministry of Housing and the real estate portal Idealista (which typically lists nearly half a million homes) reported price increases ranging from 30%–40% nationwide, going up to 70% in high-demand areas, during the eight-year period of progressive government, exceeding even the real estate bubble that triggered a 2008 crisis coinciding with the global financial crisis. The country is only just beginning to recover from its impact.

The half-hearted measures approved in previous years to tackle the problem ran into resistance from Spain’s regional governments and city councils controlled by the opposition—the center-right Partido Popular (PP), which governs 13 of Spain’s 19 regions. “Exactly,” the mayor of Madrid, José Luis Martínez-Almeida, said on X in 2021, when opponents accused him of doing “nothing” to tackle the rental crisis in the capital, where the average rent already exceeds the minimum wage.

On October 5, following a tumultuous legislative session in a divided Congress (the more powerful of the two houses in Spain’s parliament), Sánchez announced a snap election. Two days later, Maricarmen Abascal died in the hospital.

If Sánchez loses this election—and even the most optimistic nongovernmental polls, just over a month before the election, give him only between a 5% and 10% chance of winning another term—one of the world’s last bastions of social democracy will disappear along with him. Perhaps the most significant one, both because of the influence Spain has gained within the EU in recent decades and because of the personal leadership Sánchez has exercised in global geopolitics, with the prime minister having spoken out on issues such as climate change; digital governance of AI; the war in Gaza; and, in recent days, European support for Ukraine and migration management. This last issue has even pitted him against another of Europe’s last remaining social democrats (who is also in a precarious coalition), Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen. “Sánchez is the last social democrat who defends a migration policy that is compatible with human rights,” explains political scientist Pablo Simón, a university professor and specialist in electoral systems and political parties, “and he is committed to feminism and environmentalism. Once he leaves office, Spain will be more in line with the majority of Europe and its governments.”

Policies that Sánchez has implemented domestically include granting ministerial status to the 2030 Agenda, elevating the energy transition and the fight against climate change to the level of vice presidency during his terms, and creating the first agencies in any EU country dedicated to AI governance. He has also boasted about these achievements in flawless English—still a novelty among Spanish prime ministers, who have not been particularly fond of languages—at numerous international events. All of this has taken place at a time when the established world order is collapsing, and he has emerged as one of the world leaders who most vocally opposes Donald Trump. When he denied Trump the use of Spanish bases to attack Iran, he directly accused the American president of using “the smoke of war to hide his failure and, in the process, line the pockets of a select few.”

But support for Gaza (not only does Spain recognize Palestine as a state, but Sánchez has also strongly denounced Israel’s actions and labeled them as genocide) and opposition to warmongering leaders like Trump do not win elections on their own. “The debates in Spain are quite similar to those across Europe and focus on the cost of living and immigration, which explain the discontent with governments in many countries,” Simón explains, painting a picture that affects social democrats like Sánchez, leaders further to his right like Macron, and even hard-liners like Giorgia Meloni. The problems of inflation, low wages, loss of purchasing power, and strains on the welfare state are taking their toll on nearly every government in Europe.

Sánchez is, in fact, something of an anomaly with his eight years of resistance—he even titled his book about his political life Manual de Resistencia (Manual of Resistance). Looking ahead to these elections, it appears, on paper, almost impossible for Sánchez to retain his leadership. But if anything has defined his political career, it’s his ability to survive at the last moment, aided by the sociological realities of Spain. Ignacio Urquizu, director of Metroscopia and an election expert, explained a few days ago on SER, Spain’s leading radio network, that it “is the most left-leaning country in Europe, surpassed only by Malta.” He also noted that, since the 1980s, “there has been a straight line” showing that 45% of Spanish society consistently identifies as left-wing or center-left.

Sánchez has always relied on that reality for his historic comebacks. He went from being forced to resign in 2016 as secretary-general of the PSOE (the Spanish socialist party), under pressure from the party apparatus, to regaining that position just two years later and becoming prime minister on the back of a no-confidence motion against corruption, the first of its kind to succeed in Spain. The then future prime minister denounced the corruption that caused “embarrassment, disbelief, and outrage.” He has since survived two elections with the odds stacked against him, without clear majorities, in a Spain that is no longer defined by parties but by blocs, where different forces compete for similar political spaces, leading to parliaments that the framers of Spain’s constitution never anticipated.

The most dramatic of these occurred in 2023, when the right was already uncorking the Champagne, and a single member of parliament tipped the balance in favor of the socialist coalition. It was a poisoned chalice, as Spain has seen: The fact that the PP leader did not become prime minister, due to his failure to reach agreements with several nationalist right parties, paved the way for an ineffective legislative session, with 11 parties and a minority government entangled in parliamentary gridlock and social measures often being blocked by the “no” votes of Sánchez’s supposed allies. This miracle of resilience, in any case, has somehow lasted until now. Even so, Narciso Michavila, president of the social-research firm GAD3, is not ready to declare victory for the right just yet, despite what the polls say: Sánchez, he stated recently, “still has appeal,” and Michavila thinks it is still possible that he will ultimately secure another term.

But there is no denying that in the last decade in Spain, electoral politics have changed. Some of his loyal supporters during the period between 2016 and 2018 are now in prison or awaiting trial for the very corruption that Sánchez denounced. Former minister José Luis Ábalos, once his greatest supporter and whom he even mentioned in the no-confidence-motion speech that eventually led to his becoming prime minister, has now been given a 24-year prison sentence for corruption. Santos Cerdán, the man tasked with reining in the Socialist Party, is awaiting his turn in the dock. The party leadership that came to tackle corruption has proven to be just as, if not more, vulnerable to the recurring cancer of Spanish politics as those they replaced. And although Sánchez boasted about how quickly these incidents were dealt with (there are ministers from the previous administration who are still under investigation for corruption), he has long been unable to boast of integrity as he once did, now that scandals have involved his close associates.

Meanwhile, alongside these proceedings, Sánchez, his party, and many of his allies are denouncing the “judicial persecution” that has extended to the prime minister’s family—his wife, Begoña Gómez, is awaiting trial on various corruption charges, which the prosecutor’s office has opposed on the grounds of insufficient evidence (she has denied the allegations); his brother, David Sánchez, is appealing a nine-year disqualification from holding public office imposed on him by a court in Badajoz for administrative misconduct, stemming from his holding a public position as a cultural manager that was allegedly created specifically for him (he has denied the allegations). Pedro Sánchez has claimed that his brother and wife are “innocent” and victims of a “harassment and bullying operation.”

The latest chapter in this series of trials and investigations surrounding Sánchez was particularly painful for his party and his base: Former Socialist Party president and prime minister of Spain from 2004 to 2011 José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero (who was very active in the last election campaign and served as a role model for Sánchez and his vision of progressivism) was indicted in spring 2026 over an alleged corruption scheme. Jewelry valued at more than a million euros, which Zapatero took months to clarify was supposedly a gift from the Saudi monarchy, was discovered during the searches and sealed his fate. (He has denied any wrongdoing.) The role model Sánchez had looked up to and who boasted of having led the least corrupt government in the history of Spain’s democracy suddenly became the first former prime minister in the country’s democratic history to testify as a defendant. The case is still in the preliminary investigation phase.

But at first, the PSOE came out in force, through press releases and statements from its leaders, to denounce the alleged act of lawfare with the phrase “Whoever can act, should act.” It was a direct quote from the former president of the Partido Popular, José María Aznar, when he attempted to rally opposition to Sánchez’s alliance with Catalan parties in 2023.

These tensions within his family and his party, and the blurring of the lines between the two that the opposition accuses him of, have also spilled over into his campaign. This has put his wife and the developments in her legal case in the spotlight. Sánchez declared he was “deeply in love with” Gómez when he threatened to resign in 2024, following the media harassment of her. “They’ve tried to break us in every way possible, and they’ve achieved exactly the opposite; today we’re more united and stronger than ever,” the prime minister told his wife. “Let them hear it loud and clear: I love you.” The prime minister and his wife’s campaign kisses date back to at least 2016, but this time the Socialist Party has taken up the cause: “We are the party of love,” declared Minister Óscar Puente, and the prime minister has even worn a T-shirt bearing the campaign slogan “La Fuerza del Amor” (“The Power of Love”).

Meanwhile, the far right is poised to become the country’s third-largest political force, now that measures to contain it have failed in Spain, as they have elsewhere in Europe. No measures have succeeded in curbing its rise—or, in cases like Italy, its success at claiming direct power. Spain has, however, long been a country that leans more to the left; it is perhaps the most socially left-leaning country in all of Europe.

“The truth is that the Iberian Peninsula as a whole leans a bit further to the left than its neighbors due to its historical legacy,” says Simón. “In fact, because of this history, socialist parties fare better in Spain and Portugal, and they also do well in the Scandinavian countries.” On the other hand, one need only look at France, where the once all-powerful Socialist Party is now politically irrelevant, to understand the situation in much of the rest of Europe, where centrist parties have lost their influence.

It was the mobilization of Spain’s historic left-leaning majority that saved the PSOE in 2023. This had repercussions in Europe: While other social democratic leaders were falling and the centrists or moderate right-wingers were losing momentum, Sánchez became the voice of a progressive Europe. Emmanuel Macron, who, with Sánchez, built a sort of Spanish-French axis within the European Union, now watches as France burns, six months before an election in which the far right is almost guaranteed to reach at least the runoff round. And all this is unfolding in the midst of what has been described as “Russiagate,” with “foreign interference in all democratic processes in the European Union, including disinformation.”

For Europe, the consequences of this electoral process have already become apparent: The Union had to decide on a far-reaching budget, which also includes the future of Ukraine—whose president has warned that the country needs an additional 70 billion euros that Europe does not currently have. This is especially true following the revelation by Poland’s foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, that the EU has been left on its own in its contribution to Ukraine’s defense and rearmament: “Since January of last year, the United States has not contributed a single cent to Ukraine’s defense. We, Europe, are doing it.” But the elections in Spain are the start of a chain of electoral contests—France and Italy will follow—that push the possibility of an agreement further out of reach. European negotiations often drag on for years, and any electoral upheaval can derail those already underway. One of Sánchez’s most loyal ministers, Luis Planas, for example, will not appear on any electoral lists so he can devote all his time in office to these negotiations: “Between now and the end of the year, the future of the common agricultural policy and the fisheries policy is at stake,” which in Spain accounts for nearly 9% of GDP through both direct and indirect contributions.

The elections will be held on November 29 amid a tense atmosphere: The right is resorting to personal attacks and AI-generated deepfakes against Sánchez, his wife, and his cabinet. Left-wing forces have not found a figurehead like Jean-Luc Mélenchon of the France Insoumise (France Unbowed) party and are polling at less than 10%—a situation that would leave the PSOE without strong coalition partners even if it performs well. Sánchez’s international standing and the strength of the macroeconomy will likely have little weight in an election where the focus is on basic issues including the cost of living and specifically housing. But whatever the outcome, it will likely be the first in a series of elections that may lay bare the crisis facing liberal democracies in Europe. Now without the protection of the United States, it faces two existential crises. There’s an internal crisis, marked by the rise of the far right and its contempt for human rights, and an external crisis, with the Russian threat becoming clearer by the day and commercial and technological pressure from the United States and China, which has counted Sánchez among its most important advocates in its dealings with Europe.

#3744. Nexus Mods introduces new AI disclosure rules, but won't ban AI mods outright

"We hope what we have planned for now is a good first step."

Nexus Mods, the largest website for finding and downloading PC mods, has revealed new guidelines aimed at properly identifying mods created entirely using gen-AI or those created with AI assistance.

In a new blog post, Nexus clarified its stance on a number of topics, but said it won't ban AI-generated mods altogether. Going forward, mod authors are required to disclose whether or not their mods used AI, and clarify how it was used. A toggle has also been added, giving visitors of the site the ability to filter out any mods that use AI.

Aware of how controversial the decision not to have a blanket AI ban would be, site co-owner Foledinho explained that although "we are pro-human creativity", it would be "difficult to draw a clear boundary between what is acceptable and unacceptable".

"An outright ban will not eliminate AI from the modding process but will prevent people from mentioning its use," Foledinho explained. "We'd prefer the opposite; it should be out in the open, clearly labelled, and regulated according to the rules that we can implement on our platform."

That same courtesy extends to mods created entirely using AI, so long as that fact is disclosed. "This doesn't mean that any work done using AI will get removed; AI-generated mods are welcome on our platform provided that they meet certain criteria regarding permissions, transparency, presentation, and conduct," the post continues.

The new, mandatory disclosures cover existing mods, too, whose authors have 60 days to review whether their mods meet the new requirements. The new rules come alongside updates to the site's UI, which should make AI tags on mod pages more prominent. Not all backend changes will arrive at once, however.

"While we hope these changes will encourage everyone to disclose their AI usage, to be honest, that's not going to happen," Foledinho added. "Additionally, we are putting clear moderation standards in place, enforced with consequences for breaking the rules."

A different (albeit related) problem the deluge of AI-assisted mods introduced is the idea of remixing and modifying other authors' mods, often without their permission.

Nexus Mods doesn't have a solution for that problem at the moment, but the site is "working on introducing new permission options covering AI usage and training, as well as forks and derivative mods." By the same token, the post clarified the site won't itself use mods to train AI, or sell or license the mods to "anyone doing so".

This could prove to be a more complex problem to solve, given how often one mod relies on another mod to function, and that's saying nothing of contributions from other authors or users themselves.

Then there's the issue of AI-generated and AI-assisted thumbnails, which run the gamut from those entirely created by gen-AI to original shots upscaled or enhanced using AI tools. The post said no new rules governing those cases are being introduced, calling them "grey zones", but that "this discussion is not over yet."

"I'll be honest with you all, there are some details we still need to figure out and work through, especially when it comes to existing licences, forks, and how permissions apply to different versions of a mod," the post goes on. "But we want to get this right, and not rush through changes that could cause more problems further down the line. This does mean that these improvements will take longer to deliver, but we hope what we have planned for now is a good first step, and you'll bear with us whilst we continue to move in the right direction."

Just yesterday, indie game website itch.io was forced to expand its AI disclosure filter as 'AI slop' threatened to overwhelm the site. Previously, Valve came under pressure due to a perceived lack of curation around AI-developed titles during the most recent Steam Next Fest, prompting public outcry and a demand for more action from the company.

A chain of events that led to a record-breaking $6.3 billion mega-hack began with a dodgy download, so says the company that was hacked, Binance.

The world's largest cryptocurrency exchange says that the hack was not a "single isolated breach or simple phishing incident"; multiple steps were required to break through its security measures. It all began when a Wallet DevOps engineer (named Engineer A) downloaded a tampered Homebrew installation that was suggested to them by an unnamed search engine.

Homebrew is a third-party package manager for macOS. A report from the SANS Technology Institute, linked to in Binance's investigation, suggests that malicious adverts for Homebrew have been spotted in search engine results, hoping to ensnare users into installing malware on a user's PC.

"Our security team detected the anomaly, replaced the device, and rotated all related credentials as a proactive security action," Binance says. "However, Engineer A’s role and his related colleagues on our wallet infrastructure team was exposed to the hacker."

Then came a separate incident with a software engineer (named Engineer B). They were contacted through a job hunting platform (Binance says it was a legitimate platform) and was asked to attend a first-round interview with a HR representative. This was followed by up a second-round interview with the CEO. Not the HR representative, nor the CEO, however, were real; the company was made up.

The aim of the interviews? To offer Engineer B an 'assignment' that was really a repository of malicious code that executed during setup. The malware ran a series of commands and evasion techniques to avoid detection, thus avoiding Binance's security checks.

The attacker used Engineer B's now-compromised computer and an internal AI tool to gain control over two further machines: that of Engineer A and another Wallet Software engineer (Engineer C). They discovered a container deployment permission token on Engineer A's machine. With this, they could log into Engineer C's computer using the stolen credentials to create a container and trigger a malicious script to start the mega-hack that would drain $6.3 billion worth of funds from wallets used to store transitory funds by the exchange.

So, basically, the internet is a bad place, and you can't trust anyone. Or, at least, you have to have your wits about you—especially if you happen to have the key to a multi-billion dollar company's finances stored on your PC somewhere. Luckily, my PC is just pictures of my cat and a Steam backlog that won't quit.

That's actually some of the criticism levelled at the company. Should it have been possible to get this level of access even with spoofed ads and jobs?

TLDR: If DPRK are reading this, they should be saying "time for round 2". Takeaways: - critical infra engineers are free to download arbitrary software on work laptops. - the day-to-day work setup can connect to billion dollar signing environments. - no human oversight or physical confirmation for moving 10-figs of value / EIP-7702 code change. - various AI vibe-based tools running in corp environments doing god knows what except serving as a remote compromise surface, framed as a good thing btw. - none of the above labelled as the problem. - instead, reads as blaming employees for falling for social engineering, and anti-virus not catching the malware. This is a dog-ate-my-homework level excuse deployed after a nuclear-failure level event. Sincerely hoping binance have more reloads available to cover the next losses too. Reaching exchange hot wallets will never be near impossible, but it should not be this easy either.November 3, 2026

And here's Binance co-founder Yi He on taking that criticism...

Regarding criticism and suggestions about Binance’s security and access management, we accept them all. We have always believed that transparency builds trust. We read every comment one by one. Binance is not a perfect company, but a company that is constantly evolving. Criticism shows that people have expectations and standards for Binance, and these are sources of motivation for our growth. Binance has never shirked responsibility where problems exist. At present, as a trading platform, Binance needs to address three issues: 1）Will users’ funds be affected? Binance will bear full responsibility，this is what we should do. Legally, if the funding gap is large, one could file for bankruptcy and run away, but Binance operates in a “user-centric” way, with contractual spirit and a sense of moral responsibility. 2）How did the problem occur? Before publication, many professionals advised that it would be best not to include details, but we believe transparency creates trust. If this report is of reference value to other peers regarding the complexity of social engineering and the warning about AI permission boundaries, then the report is meaningful. 3）How can it be prevented in the future? We have already restructured security boundaries across departmental access management, security environments, updated devices, reset AI tools, and in accordance with zero-trust and least-privilege principles. A security audit will subsequently issue a report. Finally, we welcome more top AI security experts and technical talent to join Binance. You can DM me directly or apply on the Binance website for positions you are interested in. Joining Binance to verify this security system is the best way to validate it. 关于对币安的安全和权限管理的批评建议，我们都认。我们一直相信坦透明会建立信任，大家的评论都有一条一条看，币安不是完美的公司，但是一个一直在进化的公司，批评说明对币安有期望，对币安有标准，这些都是我们成长的动力源泉。 币安有问题的地方也从来没有推卸过责任。当下，币安作为交易平台需要解决三个问题： 1）用户的钱会不会受影响？币安会完全承担，这是我们应该做的。法律上资金缺口大可以申请破产跑路，但币安经营是“以用户中心”，是契约精神和大义。 2）问题是怎么发生的？发布前很多专业人士的意见是最好没有细节，但我们认为透明产生信任，如果这个报告在社会工程的复杂度，在AI权限边界的警示对其他同行有参考意义，那么这个报告就有意义。 3）以后如何杜绝？当前已经从各部门权限管理，安全环境，更新设备，重置AI工具，并遵循0信任、最小化原则重构安全边界，后续会由安全审计出具报告。 最后欢迎更多顶尖的AI安全专家和技术人才加入币安，您可以直接DM我本人，也可以在币安网站申请你感兴趣的岗位。加入币安来验证这套安全体系是最好的验证办法。November 4, 2026

#3742. How Early Did DWTS' Pasha Pashkov and Amber Glenn Start Planning for Finale?

Dancing With the Stars pro Pasha Pashkov and partner Amber Glenn revealed how early they started planning their finale routine during their season 35 journey.

“Semifinals is only, like … we have next week’s dance, and then it’s semifinals,” Glenn, 27, exclusively told Us on Monday, November 2, after a successful quickstep during Disney Night.

When asked whether the pair had already started brainstorming ideas, Pashkov, 40, replied, “Yeah” but played coy about what that entails.

“Before the first even dance, you start thinking [about] what could happen. You have to plan,” Glenn chimed in. “Oh, the plans change. I’m not saying that we come up with a plan and we stick to it. Plans change.”

Pashkov confirmed that he does have “thoughts” about what they’ll do if they make it to the finale, but teased, “Oh, you can’t say thoughts.”

Glenn didn’t reveal too much either, telling Us that she and Pashkov have “always seen inspiration everywhere.”

The Olympic figure skater explained, “There’s always a, like, ‘Look what I saw. Oh, look what I saw. Oh, look at this.’ And we’re always just showing each other things that we like. ‘Cool, this works, this works, this works.’”

Pashkov nodded his head as Glenn continued, saying that they have “weeks and weeks” of back and forth between them on their vision board.

“[For] freestyle, there aren’t, you know, nearly as many rules versus, like, we’re doing a style every week. So it’s like, ‘OK, well, maybe we’ll save that for this,’” Glenn shared. “So we have a lot of, ‘Maybe we’ll save that for this.’ And please vote so we can get to it.”

While Pashkov and Glenn need fan votes to make it all the way to the November 24 finale, they found success and impressed guest judge Cynthia Erivo on Tuesday’s broadcast.

The duo kicked off the show with a quickstep to “A Star Is Born” from Hercules, earning a score of 34 out of 40.

“I just thought that was the most joyful thing ever to start this with,” Erivo, 39, told the dancers. “The strength that you both have is just glorious to watch. … Well done.”

Glenn told Us after the show that she doesn’t like seeing her scores “go lower,” but she tries not to think about it because each week she has different dances to master. (The pair earned a 36 and a 38 the two previous weeks.)

Instead, the Olympic gold medalist is focused on the journey and staying present after finding a different side of herself on DWTS.

“One, I’m doing something completely different [than ice skating], and two, I’m surrounded by new people that now I can’t imagine life without,” Glenn said. “So it’s a transformation I couldn’t be more grateful for, and I want to stay in it. I wish it was longer.”

Pashkov noted that Glenn told him earlier that day, “This is my life now. What do I do after this?” adding that his dance partner has gotten “super used to the schedule [and] the flow of things.”

Glenn was in total agreement, pointing out that she wants people to vote, not because she thinks, “‘Oh, my God, I need to win the championship.’ No, I just want to, one, do [Pasha] justice and two, just keep doing this.”

Dancing With the Stars airs on ABC and Disney+ Tuesdays at 8 p.m. ET.

Now that the spooky season has officially ended, a certain celebrity family is already decked out in their favorite Christmas attire and bringing in a stylish cheer that’ll last until New Year. The Kardashian-Jenner brood have traded scary movies and creepy costumes for a holiday campaign that brought (nearly) the whole family together. Just two days out from Halloween, the stars are already bringing what they call "SKIMSmas" to the forefront.

This isn’t the first time the famous sisters have come right out of Halloween launching a Christmas-themed campaign for Kim Kardashian’s SKIMS brand. A few years ago, they did a whole photoshoot with a polar bear, and this year fans have been treated to a 1970s inspired vintage photoshoot for the brand's 2026 Holiday Shop that brought Kim together with her sisters, Khloé and Kourtney Kardashian, and half-sisters Kylie and Kendall Jenner. Khloé shared her portion of the campaign on Instagram, and honestly, this is hitting me in my holiday feels:

A post shared by Khloé Kardashian (@khloekardashian)

I’m just loving the nostalgia in the campaign, especially with Khloé’s red and white onesie, paired perfectly with white gloves and boots. There’s a "kid on Christmas" feel to the video due to her sneaking up on Santa and shaking presents under the tree. (Also, don’t think I didn’t catch her being a little Grinch-y by mimicking two of the Dr. Seuss character's iconic moves.)

However, while Kardashian was distracting herself from Halloween, I was almost distracted by Dick Van Dyke's voice. The media personality’s post features a few lines from Mary Poppins. In the 1964 movie, Van Dyke stops his performance of his “One Man Band” to sing that he feels “like somethin’ is brewin’ and ‘bout to begin.” Now, the change in the wind that he feels signals the return of Julie Andrews’ titular nanny, but Kardashian is using the beloved lyrics to signal the return of Christmas. (An act usually done by Mariah Carey’s “All I Want For Christmas Is You.”)

That aside, I’m also not the only one that’s loving this campaign. Fans have called it "cinematic," but what really caught my eye was a sweet comment from Khloé's mom, Kris Jenner:

The cutest Santa’s helper I ever did see 🎅🏽🤶

Kardashian is definitely giving Mrs. Claus vibes and is clearly having fun with the festive fashion. This is only the most recent stage in the Kardashian-Jenner fashion evolution we’ve seen this year. Just a few months ago, the sisters sported some summer-friendly looks and are now trading those in for some autumn-inspired attire. (Just check out Kim wearing a bunch of brown leather to promote the opening of a new SKIMS London store.)

I wasn’t expecting to skip straight to Christmas before the turkey’s even in the oven. However, I also shouldn’t be surprised by all this, as the Kardashians are known to indulge in fun, flirty and stylish seasonal campaigns.

Kylie Jenner actually beat her sisters to the Christmas punch with a winter kissed cosmetic collection she promoted on her Instagram. The limited time collection features “four best-selling formulas, reimagined in the signature winter kissed pink.” Jenner even promoted the collection while wearing blush pink lingerie and a Christmas hat. She’s proving that, once again, she has a full Christmas dance card as she’s continuing to bring in the holiday cheer with products available through her KHY brand. The holiday wear features a black, white, pink, and olive color scheme for a more Kardashian/Jenner-esque aesthetic.

See if you can spot some SKIMS fits or fun holiday looks in Season 8 of The Kardashians, which hit the 2026 TV schedule in early October and will continue into December. New episodes can be watched every Thursday with a Hulu subscription.

#3740. Halo and Destiny composer Marty O'Donnell loses his race for a seat in the US House of Representatives

Halo and Destiny composer Marty O'Donnell's political aspirations have hit a roadblock following last night's US mid-term elections. O'Donnell was campaigning for a seat in the US House of Representatives, running as a Republican candidate in Nevada's Third Congressional District, but is projected to lose.

The Associated Press called the race at 9am this morning, with incumbent Democrat Susie Lee currently holding 59.1 percent of the vote as of writing. O'Donnell currently has 38.6 percent of the vote, making a deficit of over 51,000 votes. The Associated Press estimates 86 percent of the vote has been counted, which if accurate, would make O'Donnell's comeback impossible. Lee seems to have ridden the 'blue wave' that has seen a huge number of seats across US Congress and Senate flip over to the Democrats.

O'Donnell, who is perhaps still best known for his music work, composed many of developer Bungie's most beloved soundtracks, creating music for the likes of Halo, Destiny, Myth, and Oni. He entered the political arena following his firing by the studio in 2014. Since then, he's been a figure of some controversy, describing LGBTQA+ people as an "existential threat" alongside Marxism and Islamists. He has also spoken out against same-sex marriage equality, and his comments drew understandable scrutiny during his recent campaign.

Per his website, O'Donnell was campaigning on a platform of economic improvement, small business support, increased border security, and anti-corruption measures. He did not claim corporate Political Action Committee (PAC) money - a hot topic this election cycle - but did receive financial support from the Trump-tied Safety and Affordability Super PAC, which notably pulled $2m in funding last month.

Following his departure from Bungie, O'Donnell won a substantial settlement from the developer after claiming he was fired "without cause". In a related 2021 judgement, O'Donnell was found in contempt of court after uploading Destiny assets to his personal YouTube channel.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

"Over the course of Beta, we came to the realization that trying to hold ourselves roughly to Classic power budgets for each class meant that every new element we added needed to come at the expense of something else. Those reductions left some iconic abilities feeling lackluster, and closed the door to other potentially exciting design options."

"So over the last two weeks, we’ve raised damage on classes across the game, and have increased the health of higher level creatures to compensate. This additional 'headroom' has allowed us to tune things to a place that we hope feels better overall," via the official WoW forums.

This honestly makes the most sense to me—yes, there are some elements of Classic I want WoW: Forever to preserve. The slower, more relaxed pace and the time-to-kill (something that has been maintained to a deliberate, intentional degree) of oldschool MMOs, for one.

But if you're gonna do Classic+, you shouldn't have to limit yourself to the power and ability budgets that came out 20 years ago. You might as well go whole-hog and try to get things feeling a little more interesting, if still along the lines of that vanilla feeling.

The statement linked above, which was posted in a series of pre-release patch notes, continues: "Beyond that, some of this round of changes reflects areas where we were likely hasty in turning to Burning Crusade or Wrath-era solutions rather than carving out new ones that better fit into the Forever combat model.

"Our aim in class design is not perfect numerical equality, but rather for every class to feel valuable to the groups they join, with powerful, unforgettable moments brought on by mastering them. In Forever this is accomplished by doubling down on the strengths and differences that make each class unique, rather than overly unifying them."

Hear hear! Homogenisation is the death of interesting class design, and I've certainly played MMOs where that's been a massive problem (I am very much hoping that FF14's Evolved job reworks hit this mark). The patch notes themselves are interesting, too.

For starters, tanks have had their threat bonuses absolutely ramped. Warriors' defensive stance has spiked from a 30% to an 80% increase and Druid's bear form has been bumped from 50% to 115%, with similar threat generation buffs for Paladins. This is primarily to offset the removal of Blessing of Salvation, which seems smart to me—you probably shouldn't be balancing threat generation writ large over the spell of one class.

Rogues now have an ability called "Shank", an off-hand weapon energy generation tool—which has a different flavour for each specialisation. Combat rogues get more energy from it, Subtlety rogues can get extra combo points, and Assassination rogues can use it to debuff enemies to make them more vulnerable to their poisons.

This is just skimming the top of the iceberg—there have been a ton of changes: "We’ve used the data and feedback gathered during Beta testing to get everything tuned to a reasonable place. However, the only true test of that tuning is the game itself. With the exception of bugs and serious outliers, we don’t plan on making big tuning changes between now and the opening of the raids next month.

"Once we have sufficient data from players leveling past 30 and engaging in a wide range of content, we expect that we will do a large tuning pass based on our data. And this is all merely a starting point for the classes in Forever, which will continue to evolve over the course of the months and years ahead just as they did following the original launch in 2004."
