#3701. Phantom Blade Zero Put Up Some Massive Sales Numbers

Developer S-Game's action-RPG Phantom Blade Zero launched on October 29 and had a massive start across PC and PS5.

The game sold more than 4 million copies over its first 72 hours. That works out to 926 units sold per minute or about 15.4 per second over the first three days.

"Thank you everyone from the bottom of our hearts for all the love and support," the studio said in a social media post.

The 4 million figure counts copies sold across both PC and PS5--the game is not available on Xbox. The game reached a record of 833,921 peak concurrent users on Steam on November 1.

The game's developer is based in China, and the majority of preorders for the game came from China, Taiwan, and Hong Kong.

Phantom Blade Zero's sales out of the gate are strong, but do not come close to another hit game from the Chinese game developer scene, Black Myth: Wukong. That game sold 10 million copies over its first three days. The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom, meanwhile, sold 10 million copies in three days as well.

If you’re looking to get started, you can check out our Phantom Blade Zero guides hub for many walkthroughs on increasing your power and finding rare items.

“S-Game’s Wuxia-inspired combat puts you in the middle of a Chinese action movie,” Richard Wakeling wrote in GameSpot’s Phantom Blade Zero review.

#3699. When Is Resident Evil Coming To Home Video? It Could Be Very Soon

Zach Cregger's Resident Evil movie crushed it at the box office, banking more than $400 million globally to become the most successful entry in the series ever. When will the film be available to watch at home, though?

According to Fandango, the home video release is set for November 3. That's apparently when people can buy the movie outright or rent it digitally, with a physical edition for Blu-ray coming at some point later. It will also presumably come to streaming at some point, and it should hit Netflix given the multi-billion-dollar Pay-1 deal the two companies have in place.

While we wait, Netflix just announced that director Paul W.S. Anderson's original Resident Evil, along with its follow-up, Resident Evil: Apocalypse, are now available to stream.

They join the other Resident Evil movies already on Netflix, including Resident Evil: Afterlife, Resident Evil: Retribution, Resident Evil: Extinction, and Resident Evil: The Final Chapter. The 2022 Resident Evil TV show is also currently streaming on Netflix.

While the new Resident Evil movie may be coming to home video on November 3, it's also staying in theaters. In fact, it was just announced that the movie is returning to IMAX and other premium large format (PLF) screens.

Cregger, who co-wrote and directed the new Resident Evil movie, recently discussed the backlash from the hardcore gamer community. He said he should have known better that fans of the games wouldn't embrace him and his ideas. After the movie came out and got great reviews and made tons of money, Cregger said he felt "gratified."

The filmmaker has said he has ideas for more Resident Evil movies, but he's not going to pursue them; instead, he's only going to make original, non-franchise movies going forward. His next movie, The Flood, is a sci-fi film starring Jennifer Lawrence.

#3698. 31 Moments That Made The Dragon Age Series Unforgettable

BioWare’s closure last month has put a lot of focus on the Mass Effect series, as the shutdown also coincided with the cancelation of the fifth game in the studio’s sci-fi series. But the company’s fantasy series,Â Dragon Age, also deserves some eulogizing. All fourÂ Dragon Age games are vastly different, spanning different RPG frameworks, fantasy subgenres, and corners of the world of Thedas. Though BioWare left some dangling threads at the end ofÂ Dragon Age: The Veilguard, it also seemed like the studio was focusing on narrative closure, just in case this was the last time anyone in the studio would get to go back to the universe it had created over four games and 15 years. With BioWare gone, let’s look back at some of the best moments from all four games.

Dragon Age: Origins begins with one of six playable opening chapters, the one you play based on the race and class of character you choose, providing a unique background for your character before they head out into the main story.

The Hero of Ferelden can be part of human nobility facing a tragic series of losses, a castless dwarf struggling to make it in the city of Orzamar, or a mage evicted from the magic school theyâve known their entire life, and those starkly different origin points are only half of the options. These origins define how your hero will be viewed in the dozens of hours that follow, and also function as a starting point for how a new player will view the franchise. I started as a Mage when I first played Dragon Age: Origins in 2009, and have always felt like a veteran of the Circle at heart. Future Dragon Age games would implement this concept of different player backgrounds with Inquisition and The Veilguard, but none would do it as thoroughlyâOrigins was the only time I got to see that history play out in real-time.

No character in Origins is as impactful as Morrigan, the enigmatic Witch of the Wilds. The apostate carries a sense of superiority toward the rest of the party, as well as the trials and tribulations of Thedas. When you meet her in the early hours of Origins, you still donât know much about the world, but her commanding presence elevated by Claudia Blackâs excellent voice performance tells you that she is unlike anyone or anything youâve met so far. Morrigan is one of the few characters in Dragon Age who watches nearly every important moment in Thedasâ history unfold, so seeing her here, both enigmatic but still so young and naive, is chilling to look back on.

After youâve picked your background and lived out whatever trauma is associated with it, Dragon Age: Origins puts you at the center of a battle with a darkspawn horde. Your job is to signal for reinforcements to help defeat an army of bloodthirsty monsters, but before the battle starts, the vibes seem off. The golden retriever King Cailain is jazzed about the incoming battle, though his father-in-law Loghain Mac Tir seems less enthusiastic. The tension between the two is tangible, but who are you to get involved in royal family affairs? However, when you signal for reinforcements, Loghain instead commands his forces to retreat, leaving everyone, including you and his own son-in-law, for dead at the hands of the Blight. Most of the preceding origin stories are full of some kind of betrayal. You might think you would get some respite from it at some point, but Origins doubles down, reminding you that you know nothing of this world and the lengths people will go to get what they want.

Origins is not an entirely grimdark fantasy dramaâsome of the best character interactions come from your party members hanging out with your dog companion. Though Mabari dogs are trained to be vicious combatants, your canine companion is a sweetheart. Many interactions between the party and dog give him a hard time for being a mangy mutt, only for him to be revealed as a sensitive soul who just wants to play. Examine your preconceived notions, Origins crew. The sharp fangs mask that the Mabari is actually a good boy.

There are several points in the Dragon Age series in which a party member can turn on you, but none have ever been quite as shocking as when the religious bard Leliana, and otherwise kind-hearted Wynne, turn on you if you taint the Urn of Sacred Ashes. This is a crime against one of the most prominent doctrines in all of Thedas, and bringing two of the most devout members of the party to watch is bound to cause drama, but Origins takes it a step further by having both of your teammates take up arms against you.

It doesnât matter how far youâve progressed through their personal stories, or even if youâre involved in a romance with Leliana; faith trumps all other emotions here, and you will have to strike down your allies. Youâll face plenty more betrayals during the Dragon Age series, but Leliana and Wynneâs heel turn is still one of the most sudden and violent.

Much like killing Leliana, Origins has a few choices whose ramifications were so earth-shattering that BioWare later had to write themselves out of the box theyâd created so they could re-use characters that could be dead. One of those was the option to kill Flemeth, Morriganâs even more enigmatic mother who allegedly wanted to steal her daughterâs body as a vessel to live longer, though the reality is a bit more nuanced than that. When Morrigan finds out about this plan, she begs you to slay the old woman in her hut in the woods. You can choose to do so or strike a deal with her to spare her in exchange for her grimoire of old spells, but choosing to slay her means fighting her in a powerful dragon form. Itâs a tough fight, but doing so leaves you not with a rewarding cutscene and major story revelation, but instead an unsettling and anticlimactic quiet. Youâre left with more mysteries than you had when you arrived, and the unshakable feeling that you might have killed something far beyond your understanding. Flemethâs place in the Dragon Age universe was too significant to be silenced by something as trivial as death, but for a moment, you feel like you have driven a stake through the heart of something you cannot comprehend.

Dragon Age: Originsâ big moment where all your choices culminate is The Landsmeet, a political meeting where you can finally unmask Loghain for all his crimes and essentially set up the country of Fereldenâs future. Your relationships and understandings formed over the past 50+ hours of video game are put to the test, and things can change drastically depending on how the battles of wits and blades pan out. To this day, The Landsmeet is one of BioWareâs most effective showcases of its ability to sew hours of choices into a final consequence. In just one quest you solidify the future for Ferelden in a way that sends most players down the same path, but colors that result so differently that many players, especially those who donât know every secret the game has to offer, will see something that diverges significantly from what the next player might see.

One of the last major choices youâll make in Dragon Age: Origins comes back to Morrigan. The witch has had more than enough reasons to leave the party considering she doesnât really get along with anyone on the team, but she sticks around long enough to give you a final choice: ending the Blight will cost you your lifeâunless you or Alistair undergoes a blood magic ritual that will transfer the Archdemonâs soul into an unborn child. It sounds like a get-out-of-jail-free card, all you have to do is lay with her for one night or convince Alistair to do it. But Morrigan is cagey with her intentions and says that whether you agree or not, she will leave the party after the final battle. This is why sheâs been here this whole time, but does that mean any connection youâve formed with her was all an act? What will become of this child? Is it going to be like any other child or will it be some darkspawn demon that could bring about just as much pain in the world as the archdemon would? Morrigan gives you nothing to go on, but makes her terms clear. Dragon Age: Origins would go on to have three sequels that would wipe away the ambiguity of this decision, but at the time, all you had to go on here was your trust of Morrigan, or lack thereof. Everything youâve ever been told about blood magic and interrupting the natural order of the Blight should tell you to say âno,â but are you willing to risk it to save your own life? Itâs a fascinating choice. Did Dragon Age do right by it? Your mileage may vary.

With Dragon Age II, BioWare started earnestly looking for a way to franchise the series. It had built itself a new cage as the âchoice and consequenceâ studio thanks to the Mass Effect series, and Dragon Age followed suit by importing your Origins save to pepper in cameos and references to your past deeds. That includes whether or not you killed Flemeth, but since BioWare still wanted to use the mysterious witch either way, it had new hero Hawke unwittingly carry her to safety through an enchanted amulet even as she fought for her life against the Hero of Ferelden. Reviving Flemeth is one of the most effective moments in all of Dragon Age in showing how playing as different protagonists in each game could create satisfying meta moments. As she rises from the ashes, you watch the impact of one of your heroâs actions be undermined by the one youâre playing as now. Dragon Age takes place over decades, and a big part of its appeal is watching different stories youâve helped write weave in and out of one another. Itâs a course correction, but one that is still bone-chilling to watch unfold.

The second Dragon Age differs from the first in several ways, from taking place almost entirely in one city to swapping the tactical RPG battle system for more action-oriented combat. But one of the most notable and interesting changes it made was to the approval system, which integrated a Friendship and Rivalry mechanic so you didnât have to kiss a party memberâs ass to progress their relationship storyline. The difference between Friendship and Rivalry is all about how you challenge their preconceived notions. Each party member has a pretty defined view of the world; the radical mage Anders, for instance, is all about freeing magic users from the Circle at any cost, while the elven slave Fenris has an aversion to magic. Uncritically enabling them will give you Friendship points, and going against the grain will net you Rivalry points. This changes the tone of your relationships significantly, and even someone youâre in a romantic relationship with may greet you with a thorny disposition. Watching those connections gradually change is one of the most compelling parts of Dragon Age IIâs writing. Romancing Fenris as a mage while being rivals was one of the most interesting, angsty relationships Iâve ever experienced in a BioWare game. Itâs a shame the studio didnât keep the system around.

Dragon Age II is all about years of civil unrest bubbling to the surface of one city, and between the conflict with the stranded Qunari and the Mage/Templar War, the former is certainly handled with more care than the latter. While early Dragon Age games had multiple crisis points in which party members can leave the party or betray you, one of the most memorable is when one party member makes a decision not to leave, but to return. Isabela is the cause of the Qunariâs extended stay in Kirkwall, and when sheâs given the chance to run off with a tome they have been searching for, she takes it. If youâve not established a solid enough friendship or rivalry with her, she will never return. If you have, she makes a big heroâs entrance just as the Qunari are about to strike down what remains of the city. She attempts to make amends, showing the growth sheâs been trying her damnedest to avoid since arriving in the city. But then the Qunari leader says she still must answer for her crimes. You can give her up and betray her, or you can fight for her instead, and seeing her be big enough to not sell you and the rest of Kirkwall out for once in her life is one of Dragon Age IIâs most memorable companion moments.

Choosing to fight for Isabelaâs freedom results in a somewhat silly but exceptionally satisfying fight. Dragon Age IIâs action-based combat isnât quite as snappy and tight as The Veilguardâs, but it has some spectacle that can keep it interesting in fights that donât just pit you against waves of enemies being thrown at you. The Arishok fight can go a few ways depending on if he respects Hawke or not, but fighting the giant Qunari in a one-on-one duel is still one of the best combat sequences in the game. You may be in for a tough time if you havenât specâd into a class and build that can handle a solo fight, but in any case, taking down the Arishok and being crowned the Champion of Kirkwall is one of the defining moments of Dragon Age II

One bright spot in Dragon Age IIâs extremely uneven final act is the conclusion to Merrillâs story. The elven blood mage has gone against the wishes of everyone around her in a tunnel-visioned need to bring back a part of her clanâs history, even seeking out the help of a demon. Dragon Age II takes place across a decade, with Merrill at odds with her clan leader Marethari all the while, and yet the leader sacrifices herself to âsaveâ Merrill by allowing the demon she had been working with to possess her instead. Merrill can insist this was meddling and you can be supportive of her or not, but the real people she has to answer to are the clanâs remaining members. Depending on whether you advocate for her or throw her under the bus, you may have to fight the entire clan on your way out. Itâs a brutal mess thatâs tied to the character with perhaps the most emotional range of any party member in the franchise. Itâs such a terrifying, saddening web of contradicting feelings and subverted expectations, all leading to a stunning payoff.

I have a lot of issues with the handling of the Mage/Templar War in Dragon Age II. It creates this complicated political and religious conflict around an oppressed group of people and a tyrannical religious organization but insists that both sides are equally bad, actually. Donât even get me started on how you can convince Anders, the radical mage who is the face of this conflict, to kill the mages he tried to save. But the moment in which Anders, worn down by a lifetime of captivity and oppression, blows up the Kirkwall Chantry is one of the few unambiguous statements the game makes in its final hours. The scene itself is dramatic and shocking and kickstarts a war that would (in theory) shake the foundations of Thedas. It requires everyone in your party to make a stand. There will be no more fence-sitting in this fight, and all your relationships will be tested as your team decides whether or not to follow you into battle. Sadly, the reveals that follow undermine any choice you make, but as a spark that ignites a flame, Andersâ act of terrorism is a statement in a game that otherwise seems unwilling to make one.

A lot of the highlights weâve talked about are big story moments or reactions to your decisions, but one of the coolest things Inquisition does happens literally the moment the game starts. The main menu shows rows of mages and templars marching toward a building off in the distance. Despite where we left them in Dragon Age II, these two opposing sides donât seem to be fighting, so perhaps theyâre making their way to peace talks? Could the future of Dragon Age be written not in blood, but in signed treaties? Letâs press ânew gameâ and find o-

I have heard some fans say the moment in which members of the Inquisition start singing âThe Dawn Will Come,â a hymn of the Chantry, to your main character in a moment of religious fervor is cheesy and cringe, to which I say, fuck you, itâs one of the most incredible moments in the game. Inquisitionâs themes can be radically different depending on how you play the Herald of Andraste. This hero has been unwillingly made a religious figure, with hundreds of people expecting you to live as a symbol for a god you might not even believe in. If you take this approach, playing as a non-believer who actively shouts down the claims of the faithful, âThe Dawn Will Comeâ can be an unnerving, haunting reminder of how much unwavering belief can compel groups of people even as you insist on a different, provable truth. If, on the other hand, youâre undecided or playing as a believer, it can read like a beautiful moment of hope and community. Inquisition allows you to define so many shades of who your character is and see them reflected in a world that struggles with your very existence. And sometimes, no matter how hard you kick and scream, you cannot stop the world from believing what it does. Instead, you can just awkwardly stand there while people sing to you and then complain about it later.

With each subsequent game, Dragon Age has gotten better at illustrating the closeness (or lack thereof) of your companions. Banter in the overworld is good, but seeing the crew actually get together is better. The Wicked Grace scene, in which the party gets together to play a card game, is one of BioWareâs best scenes that make use of a gameâs entire core ensemble. Everyoneâs personality gets a chance to shine, whether theyâre playful, stuffy, horny, or just trying to wrangle all these weirdos together. Itâs delightful, succinct, and has stayed in the hearts of many Dragon Age fans.

The Dragon Age series has always been explicitly queer. For all the diaper-shitting about The Veilguardâs queer themes, Inquisition was examining the life and times of a Thedas gay long before Taash learned the term ânon-binary.â Dorian Pavusâ personal quest remains one of the most memorable in all of BioWareâs canon. It drops combat for one incredibly well-acted cutscene between the Tevinter mage and his estranged father, where itâs revealed that, to continue their bloodline and climb his way up the Tevinter political ladder, Dorianâs father planned to use a blood magic equivalent to conversion therapy in order to force his son into an arranged marriage. Iâve spoken to many Dragon Age fans over the years about what decision they made here, as youâre able to help the two reconcile, or to get Dorian out of there. Iâve never once considered telling Dorian to hear his father out. Itâs one of the best examples Iâve seen of a game adapting the queer struggle to a fictional culture. Dorian becomes a radical because he has seen how low even those he loves will go to maintain power in Tevinter, and it all ties into his identity as a gay man. Itâs a stunning scene that tells you so much about Dorian and where he came from, and lets you gently nudge history as you stand beside him.

Blackwall goes under the radar for a lot of players. Heâs quiet, keeps to himself, and is even in a pretty out-of-the-way spot in your base in Skyhold. A lot of people think the Grey Warden warrior is boring, but theyâre wrong; the big reveals you experience in his companion missions are outstanding. Blackwall tells you heâs a Warden but is secretive about the organization which, if you played Origins, may nudge you to think back to your own experience playing as one. You know why theyâre all tight-lipped on the inner machinations of the faction, so you donât question it. But it turns out, heâs actually not a Warden at all, and is instead an imposter on the run for war crimes he committed years ago. Eventually, the guilt eats at him and he turns himself in to save others from answering for his orders with a hangmanâs noose. This man duped you for dozens of hours, and youâre left with the power to decide his fate. Blackwallâs quest can go one of several ways, whether you leave him to rot, pardon him, or send him to the Wardens to let them decide what happens to an imposter. Whatever you choose, Blackwallâs quest leaves an impression as one of BioWareâs most surprising and subversive. Yâall need to quit calling characters you donât even talk to boring. This shit rips.

Even as someone who likes Mass Effect more than Dragon Age, I have a hard time thinking of a singular quest in the sci-fi series that matches up to Inquisitionâs Wicked Eyes and Wicked Hearts. While you will unsheathe your weapons a few times, this mission is all about politics, charming the worst people youâve ever met, and working the crowd. Running around the Winter Palace, meeting the most powerful players in Orlais, and manipulating the politics of an entire country to your whims is more intriguing than anything you do with a sword or staff. Mechanically, the mission is surprisingly elegant as it codifies social status and attention into something that can be measured by a video game, and itâs intriguing learning more about the figureheads you can rally to your cause. There are several outcomes at the end of this mission, and getting what you want might come down to blackmail, reuniting long-lost lovers, or a betrayal of your own. Itâs unlike anything else in the Dragon Age series, and I havenât seen many studios pull off something like it since.

At one point, it seemed as if Flemeth might be the throughline connecting all of Dragon Age. For two games, she was presented as a manipulator, lurking in the shadows and moving the pieces of Thedasâ chess board to her liking. Then all her machinations finally came to a head in Inquisition when she, Morrigan, and perhaps the child the player helped conceive two games prior, all gather in the Fade. Flemeth seemingly has control of the situation, appearing to hold her grandson Kieran hostage and using him as leverage against her daughter who has been on the run since Origins. But as anger gives way to truth-telling and the moment softens, the two find not total reconciliation, but at least an understanding that neither is in danger from the other. It is a series-best performance from Black and Flemeth actor Kate Mulgrew, bringing together three games of choices and history into one incredible confrontation. Iâm still unsure how I feel about the final echoes of this moment in The Veilguard, but Flemeth and her family reuniting and acknowledging the struggle of love and fear for one another that theyâre caught in remains one of the most memorable interactions in all of Dragon Age

I could just throw the entirety of the Trespasser DLC in here and it would be in the running for best âmomentsâ in the series. The final expansion BioWare released for Inquisition in 2015 isnât just an epilogue for the RPG, but is pretty much the true ending. You say goodbye to all the companions with some silly, heartfelt scenes, engage in some politics, and fight some really memorable battles, but the meat of the DLC is in its final 10 minutes. Solas, the elven apostate who abandons your team at the very end, reveals that he is the Dread Wolf, the trickster god who led a rebellion against the rest of the elven pantheon. He plans to tear down the barrier between the real and spirit worlds, which he believes will revitalize the old world of the elves, granting them immortality once more and destroying everyone else in the process. But youâre given two choices that (before The Veilguard, at least) felt incredibly meaningful as a final word for the Inquisitor: Do you think Solas is beyond saving? And is your organization in a state to fight him? Ultimately, neither of those choices mattered in The Veilguard, despite them being imported into the game at the beginning. But back in 2015 it felt like a victory lap, a final declaration by a character you probably wouldnât get to play again.

BioWare has always been held up as a studio that spearheads inclusive design, but The Veilguard takes this one step further by letting you explicitly determine that your protagonist Rook is trans. This isnât just a cosmetic choice like giving them top surgery scars or picking a voice; it can be part of your characterâs backstory that you talk about from time to time with other characters. Few games have been this thorough about letting you define your characterâs identity, and The Veilguard approaches it with a great deal of care.

The Veilguard continues the trend, started with Mass Effect: Andromeda, of BioWare hiding some of a gameâs biggest lore reveals behind an optional collectathon, but this time they are so far-reaching and important that I canât believe some players may never see them. Collecting wolf statues throughout The Veilguard reveals Solasâ regrets. These are murals depicting memories from the elven godâs long life, and essentially write the creation myth of the Dragon Age universe. When I first played The Veilguard, I did these quests pretty late and they started to turn me around on the game entirely. I had mostly considered The Veilguard less a meal than a series of really good sides, but this was when I as a long-time fan felt like I was really eating. Each reveal was juicier and more surprising than the last, bringing connective tissue to a universe that had often felt disparate and disconnected. God, I canât believe theyâre optional.

A lot of The Veilguardâs choices are binary, but most of them are still pretty compelling. The first world-altering choice comes when you must decide which of two cities to save from incoming dragon attacks: Minrathous or Treviso. Thereâs a lot of emotion tied up in this choice, as well as tactical considerations to make. Your Rook might be from Minrathous, but pursuing a relationship with Treviso native Lucanis. You may be trying to develop partnerships with the radical Tevinter group the Shadow Dragons and feel like you should help them defend their city to not burn bridges. Whatever your reasoning and whatever the consequences, you have to choose right then and there. Your teammates are looking to you for an answer, and you realize that a mere few hours of gameplay ago you were just a contractor helping Varric track down Solas. Rookâs arc is all about them confronting the leadership role that has been thrust on them by circumstance and Varricâs expectations. This is the moment it becomes clear that they might not be cut out for the decisions they have to make, but theyâll have to learn to live with those choices one way or another.

The Mourn Watch necromancer Emmrich is The Veilguardâs best marriage of character and faction culture. He is fascinated by death because he has an all-consuming fear of the end. Emmrichâs goal is to become a Lich, an immortal keeper of the dead, willing to watch life begin and end forevermore. But as his personal quests unfold, his assistant Manfred, a reanimated skeleton, is killed in a battle with a rival Lich. Using his powers, he could bring Manfred back, but doing so would disqualify him from achieving the immortality he desires, as it would show an inability to accept death. How can you be immortal and watch everything live and die in an endless cycle if one death of a loved one compels you to defy the natural order? Iâve heard people make cases for allowing Emmrich to become a Lich, but I chose to advise him to bring Manfred back and leave Lichdom behind. The Lich order may believe his inability to leave Manfred behind as a weakness, but I saw it as an asset. Itâs proof that he loves too strongly to spend an eternity watching everyone he cares about disappear over and over again. Still, I see the argument for the other side. No other choice in The Veilguard so succinctly nails the companion-first format BioWare wanted while saying so much about the world in the process.

The Grey Warden headquarters of Weisshaupt has been referenced since the very beginning of Dragon Age, and after all those years hyping it up, our first experience of it is one hell of a followthrough. The Veilguardâs mission at the fortress is an action-packed and narratively rewarding setpiece packed with reveals about the state of the Grey Wardens and demonstrating just how much of a threat the remaining elven gods pose. Meanwhile, the drama it stirs between your team of usually harmonious heroes is a peak moment for the whole series, and holy shit, that boss fight at the end might be the most challenging BioWareâs ever created.

After you see all of Solasâ regrets, you meet a visitor in the Lighthouse: Morrigan. She gives you one last big lore dump, finally putting a bittersweet bow on the tragic story between her and her mother. She also reveals to you that the figure that has been looming over their hit-and-run relationship is Mythal, the elven god of love who once led the pantheon. Mythal is long dead, but her memories have transferred from host to host in the millennia since. Morrigan is the keeper of her memories now, and believes that if even a fraction of the old god were able to release Solas from all his regret, it might be enough to take him off this violent path. Morriganâs epilogue is introspective and melancholy, but as she directs you to one of the last pieces of Mythalâs soul trapped in the fade, all that family drama is given some meaning. The conversation in which you try to convince Mythal to help you is one of the best in The Veilguard. It branches into multiple topics, giving you several footholds to perhaps convince her that your cause is just. Who your Rook is can play into how effective you are in making your case, and if you canât persuade her, you can always fight her for her favor. Whatever route you choose, this is one of those moments in which you can feel Dragon Age history changing with every dialogue option you pick.

Dragon Age: The Veilguardâs final missions are a kind of greatest hits of BioWareâs best tricks. Itâs got everything: unavoidable sacrifice, avoidable losses determined by whether or not you know your team well enough to assign them tasks befitting their talents, and a culmination of all the strategic relationships youâve built with different factions. It might not be as interactive as Mass Effect 2âs Suicide Mission, but as a series of interlocking decisions bringing you to a myriad of mini conclusions, it far exceeds anything the studio has done in the past 20 years. I was nervous and shaking making those choices, and itâs all portrayed with a level of cinematic finesse that goes beyond anything BioWareâs done before.

When The Veilguard reaches its climax, it becomes clear that all the while, youâve been caught in a battle of ideals between Varricâs hope and Solasâ cynicism. Rook has been a pawn (no pun intended) for Solas. The elf has been manipulating them the entire time in hopes of trapping them in the Fade and resuming his plan. Heâs done this by projecting a vision of Varric who hypes Rook up until they can be cut off at the knees, falling into a state of regret so consuming it traps them within the spirit realm. Here, theyâre guided by Varric through the prison until they discover the truth: Varric died at the beginning of the game, and Solas used his image to nudge Rook along the entire game.

The reveal is incredible because you realize BioWare pulled off a Sixth Sense. No one else speaks to Varric the entire game, but heâs placed naturally enough in each scene that you donât really question that no one else responds to him. You realize that youâve been fooled by Solas just as much as Rook has, and when they mourn their mentorâs loss, theyâre effectively a stand-in for you, the Dragon Age fan. But as despondent as they might be, they still have a job to do, and Varric reminds them that theyâve done everything up to this point by themself. They donât need Varricâs guidance. They already have everything they need.

As frustrated as I was with The Veilguardâs decision to leave the Inquisitor behind for a new protagonist, this twist was what made Rook work for me. The whole game essentially emerges from Varric betting on someone to finish the job he couldnât. His belief in Rook is what keeps the game going, even as Solas tries to manipulate it to his own advantage. It may have been sad to watch Varric go from a city dwarf just trying to make it to a victim of Solasâ pride, but his belief in others lives on.

After four games, pretty much everything Dragon Age has ever been leads to one final conversation with Solas. The Veil is coming down, the rest of Thedas will be burned to ash in the aftermath, and the only way to stop it is for the trickster god himself to bind himself to it. No matter what you do, Solas will end up using his immortal life force to keep Thedas and the Fade separate. But the tenor of your decision still matters. You can knock him senseless and forcibly cast the blood magic spell to hold him there, you can trick him so his magic backfires and leave him helpless as you bind him to the Veil, or you can take the third option. Bringing Mythalâs essence out allows her to release him from her service, letting him lay down a lifetime of regret. Itâs the culmination of learning all the secrets left in this world, and once you have all that understanding, it feels like the most appropriate way to cap off a cliffhanger whose resolution weâve been awaiting for ten years.

Given everything thatâs happened to BioWare in the years following The Veilguardâs launch, what sticks out to me most is how much the game leans into finality. Closure is a key pillar of its storytelling, even if there are hints of a sequel we’ll never get. And if this is the note we had to leave it off on, I’m not upset. I hope the folks who were at BioWare at any point during the seriesâ development aren’t either.

#3697. 60 Minutes Alum On The Show’s Bari Weiss Era And One Thing She Still Finds ‘Disturbing’

How A CBS News Insider Responded After Dan Rather Criticized The Company

A Former Fox News Meteorologist Is Not Holding Back About '#MeanGirl' Megyn Kelly

Dan Rather Didn’t Hold Back About Bari Weiss And More ‘Destroying’ CBS News And 60 Minutes

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

60 Minutes looked a lot different when it returned to the 2026 TV schedule for its 59th season back in September. That was in great part due to a creative overhaul that took place over the summer and saw several key employees fired from their positions. Since then, a few of those former staffers have spoken out about their oustings and the state of the news magazine under the leadership of CBS News Editor-in-Chief Bari Weiss. Now, Cecilia Vega is sharing her take and revealing one detail that still bothers her.

Since its season premiere, 60 Minutes has been at the center of various headlines, with a number of those pertaining to low ratings compared to past seasons of the show. On top of that, there have been ongoing claims of editorial interference on Weiss’ part. Vega made such claims in July and alleged that she was pressured to exude what she considered to be bias into her stories. As for her feelings on the show now, Vega said during a talk in Washington D.C. (via The Daily Beast) that she wasn’t pleased:

It pains me. It hurts to watch, from afar. It hurts to talk to my colleagues who are still there. It hurts to see the ratings slump that is happening right now.

Regarding the ratings, it was recently reported that the October 25th broadcast of 60 drew 5.6 million viewers. That marked a notable decrease for the show, which reportedly averaged 9.1 million viewers during Season 58. Weiss recently addressed the concerns during a tech panel and asserted that the show was still doing “tremendously well.” The Free Press founder, who’s denied editorial bias, also said she’d been aiming to block out the backlash against CBS News and her changes on the previously mentioned news program.

The staff firings took place on May 28, 2026, which apparently became known as “Black Thursday” internally. On that day, Vega was fired alongside others like fellow correspondent Sharyn Alfonsi, former 60 Minutes executive producer Tanya Simon and executive editor Draggan Mihailovich. Shortly after, veteran correspondent Scott Pelley was fired as well after accusing Weiss of “murdering” the show. As for Vega, one thing still gives her pause about her exit from the series and the media company as a whole:

I still don’t know why I was fired. I was not given a reason. I was fired without cause. I just find it exceptionally disturbing.

Pelley recalled the staff meeting that was held shortly after his 60 Minutes colleagues and others were fired. The veteran newsman recalled everyone expecting Weiss to be at the meeting but were surprised to find that only series EP Nick Bilton was present. According to Pelley, employees were even more unhappy after Bilton started reading a statement from his phone without looking up at anyone. Months later, Vega seems to have a lot of respect for Pelley and others who have “held the line” or those who are still trying to at CBS:

I held the line, and Scott held the line, and Sharyn held the line, and I think people are still holding the line over there. But what they are having to go through, or what we had to go through, should never happen in a newsroom.

Questions remain in regard to what lies ahead for 60 Minutes and CBS News as a whole under Bari Weiss’ leadership. Additionally, there are more variables to consider following the merger between Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery, which has birthed Skydance. Cecilia Vega, for her part, says she’s unaware of the “endgame” and thinks “it’s a real mystery.”

He eats more pizza than the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles.

#3696. Tatyana Ali Jokes Her Sons Aren't 'Impressed' by Her 'DWTS' Performances

Tatyana Ali is improving week after week on Dancing With the Stars, but to her sons, she’s still just mom.

When asked whether her sons, Edward Aszard “Aszi,” 10, and Alejandro, 7, are “impressed” by how much she’s progressed on season 35 of the ABC competition series, Ali, 47, exclusively told Us, “No, no, no, no. Listen, no, no, no, no. They’re not. No, forget that. They’re not. I’m their mother. They’re not impressed by me.”

The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air alum noted on Monday, November 2, that her kids are still watching and they are “learning” about the world of dance.

“My son asked me, he said, ‘Mommy, what kind of dance are you doing this week?’” Ali recalled. “I said, ‘Oh, I’m doing a contemporary.’ And I said, ‘You know [my partner] Jan, Mr. Ravnik? You know, he’s a champion at contemporary dance.’”

Ali said that her oldest son was knowledgeable about the genre of dance she was describing, responding, “Oh yeah, contemporary. Isn’t that the one that’s kind of like choose your own adventure?”

Jan Ravnik chimed in telling Us, “It’s true. You can do whatever you want to do.”

Although Ali teased that her boys will always see her as their mom, she was happy to report that they are tuning in and rooting for her to take home the mirrorball trophy.

“They tell me they’re proud of me when we do our nighttime prayers,” she shared. “They’re always like, ‘Let Mommy last another week. Like, let her do a good job. Let her remember her steps.’”

The actress revealed, “It’s just a really cool experience to be able to show my kids perseverance in real time.”

Ali, who shares her two children with husband Vaughn Rasberry, admitted that while they are aware of who Ravnik, 31, is, they don’t know him that well.

“He’s been on FaceTime a couple, like maybe one or two times,” she explained, adding that her kids are in school and don’t live in Los Angeles so they don’t frequent her practices.

Ali and Ravnik have found themselves at the bottom part of the leader board for multiple weeks, but during Tuesday’s Disney Night they received their first nine of the season. Their total score was a 33 out of 40.

Judge Carrie Ann Inaba even told Ali that her storytelling made her very emotional after the pair performed a contemporary dance to “Easy As Life” from Aida with guest artist Heather Headley performing live.

“I mean, that’s the whole point of performing, whether it’s acting, dancing, singing, whatever. You want to actually touch people,” Ali told Us. “So that actually did mean a lot.”

Dancing With the Stars airs on ABC and Disney+ Tuesdays at 8 p.m. ET.

#3695. Former Xbox Exec Shares Her Side Of The Story After Mysterious Depature

Helen Chiang, the veteran Xbox staffer who got promoted in July and left the company amid mysterious circumstances just recently, has shared her side of the story--but her response doesn't close the book on this saga.

In a LinkedIn post titled "Clarity is Kindess," which itself is a reference to her former boss (and Xbox CEO) Asha Sharma's much-ridiculed and cringey mantra, said it's "not accurate" that she was "fired for a policy violation" as multiple reports said.

Chiang said she will not "turn this into a play-by-play" and reveal the specifics, but she wanted to speak out to dispel rumors. "What has been said about my departure, and what has been left unsaid, has created a picture of me that I hardly recognize."

She went on to "set the record straight" by claiming she did not leak confidential company information to the press as some had speculated. "I have never communicated with any journalist outside the limited, company-authorized interviews I’ve done as part of my job," she said, adding that this includes having no contact with any journalist who reached out to her before today to ask for her side of the story.

Chiang went on to say she did not leave Xbox to join a competitor. "You don’t spend two decades somewhere without developing a deep loyalty to the people, teams, and businesses you’ve helped build," she said

"Xbox was never just another stop in my career. My end game was always to keep building here," she said.  

That may all be true, but it's also unquestionable that people regularly spend lengthy periods of their career at one company, in high-level positions, and then move to other companies.

Third, Chiang said she "did not engage in discrimination, bullying, harassment, insider trading, embezzlement, or other fraudulent activity."

"I stand by my record: both the results I delivered and the way I have treated people throughout my career. I won’t let speculation define my character or erase that record," she said.

Chiang added that she did not leave Xbox because she was "passed over for a bigger role." She said that since having children, she became more "intentional about how I define ambition and success." She said she has purposefully not sought out bigger roles or jobs with more responsibilities; she said she hadn't interviewed for a job since 2011.

"My reputation and results paved the way for the opportunities that followed. I went where the company believed I was needed and where I could have the greatest impact," she said, adding that she did not ask to become Xbox's first-ever COO.

"I believe in fairness, accountability, and holding ourselves to the standards we expect of others. Those standards only mean something when they’re applied consistently," she said.

Chiang said she has "serious concerns" about how those standards were applied in her case, and she said those concerns "deserve to be taken seriously."

"I share this because I don’t want my departure reduced to an inaccurate story about incompetence, ambition for the next big job, or a Nelson-level scandal. My story is about staying true to your core values, especially when it is hard," she said. "That’s the legacy I hope to leave behind."

Chiang's statement doesn't spell out the specific nature surrounding her departure from Xbox, so many will naturally want more answers. Those could come in time, as Chiang said this is "not the whole story."

Another former Xbox executive, Shannon Loftis, commented on Chiang's post to say she is "Team Helen all the way." Loftis said she wonders who may have leaked the "false information" about Chiang and what their motivations may have been. In any event, she says it shows a "loss of moral character and 'clarity' in leadership at Xbox."

"A real leadership team would have relentlessly pursued the 'leaker' and taken appropriate action because 'confidential personnel matters' actually are bases for defamation lawsuits," she said. "It's a clownshow up in there and I feel terrible for anyone that still has to deal with it."

A spokesperson for Microsoft told Windows Central that the company does not “discuss individual personnel matters.”

According to a source speaking to Eurogamer, Chiang was “terminated for policy violations.” The Verge’s Tom Warren backed this up, saying Chiang was cut loose due to a “policy violation,” but the exact nature of that is unknown.

In July, Sharma announced that Chiang would become Xbox’s first-ever COO, with “end-to-end” responsibility for the financial future of Xbox’s content, hardware, platform, and services.

Chiang had worked at Microsoft for 20 years, in that time playing a key role in the creation of Xbox Live and later shepherding Mojang and the lucrative Minecraft franchise. As COO, Chiang was expected to “bring our businesses together under one operating model, making sure we make clear investment decisions, learn from our successes and failures, and hold ourselves accountable for results,” Sharma said.

For her part, Sharma said she will have an update to share on the COO position at Xbox at some point, but she didn’t divulge more.

The Xbox business was “not healthy” when Sharma took over, she said, and Chiang no doubt had a challenging road ahead of her. As for now, however, people can only speculate as to the real reason she left Xbox.

#3694. How Greg Brockman’s Wife Anna Became a Trump and MAGA Mega-Donor

It was weeks before the election and spirits were low in MAGA’s top ranks. The president’s approval ratings had plunged to historic depths. Polling suggested his endorsement had become an albatross for many of his preferred candidates. And so Donald Trump had retreated to the gilded comfort of Mar-a-Lago to attend to “matters of national importance,” including, on October 17, a candlelit dinner with some of his most loyal supporters.

At the head of the table were just four seats: Google cofounder Sergey Brin, President Trump himself, OpenAI cofounder Greg Brockman, and his wife, Anna Brockman.

Anna Brockman, Greg Brockman, President Donald Trump, and Sergey Brin during a MAGA Inc. event at Mar-a-Lago. October 17, 2026.

The Brockmans, worth nearly $30 billion, have used their wealth to become the 16th-biggest political mega-donors this midterms cycle: Last year, the couple donated a combined $25 million to MAGA Inc. and $25 million to the pro-AI super PAC Leading the Future. Greg has said that he and his wife are “single-issue donors,” their lone cause being AI, the technology he’s helped build. “It’s not popular,” he recently acknowledged, so “we really want to support politicians who really lean into [it].” And it has been “we” at each of these turns—the Brockmans working in tandem toward a shared vision of the future.

Yet despite Anna Brockman’s frequent presence amid the backdrop of this pivotal scene in history, next to nothing has previously been reported about her. When The Wall Street Journal profiled Greg Brockman in May, they wrote of his elusive wife, “She is intensely private: almost no information, including her maiden name, is available online.”

Anna Chang has an unlikely past—one that raises some new questions. How did a onetime registered Democrat and ambitious tech worker who “loves everything that positively changes the world” become the retired wife of one of the wealthiest men on earth, Donald Trump’s frequent guest, and one of the single-largest donors seeking to hasten a future where artificial intelligence is developed with minimal regulatory oversight?

Sources close to the Brockmans and to OpenAI suggested that Anna is no bystander, and is worthy of scrutiny as a significant player herself. “She’s not a silent sidekick to Greg,” says one AI industry insider. “She is a force.”

When Greg and Anna met at a Silicon Valley dinner party in 2018, Greg said they “instantly connected.” She was the daughter of Korean immigrants, and he had a long-standing reverence for Korean culture: He has a black belt in tae kwon do, and even attended Korean summer camp as a teenager, picking up some of the language. They had also both worked at the payments-software start-up Stripe in the 2010s, though their tenures never overlapped. (Both Greg and Anna Brockman declined Vanity Fair’s request for comment for this story.)

In 2015, Greg had left his position as Stripe’s chief technology officer to cofound OpenAI with 10 fellow visionaries out of his San Francisco living room. A gifted and relentless coder, he muscled his way through seemingly impossible projects in the hopes of eventually achieving artificial general intelligence, or AGI (the point when the technology can match or exceed human-level capabilities at every possible task). He sometimes clocked 90-hour workweeks. Greg’s colleagues from over the years describe him as fiercely competitive, not just with work projects but also with hobbies like running and weight lifting.

Anna was a quirky and exuberant animal lover from Texas—one source estimates she and her husband live with over 20 animals—who had worked for AmeriCorps mentoring working-class students after graduating from Wesleyan University, well known as an ultraliberal school. (In a total coincidence, I discovered midway through reporting that Anna and I had overlapped there during our college years.) When she became one of the first 100 or so employees at Dropbox, her idealism persisted. In an introduction to her new colleagues, she told them she spent her free time “taking on adventures to help save the world.”

While a source close to Anna said she doesn’t drink alcohol, sources who’ve spent time with her said she has sometimes drawn attention for her juvenile humor and unconventional manner. She “curses like a drunken sailor,” said one. Another described her as “fratty.”

Early in the Brockmans’ relationship, Anna experienced a series of mysterious health mishaps. The couple spent years visiting doctor after doctor, and eventually discovered she had Hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (hEDS). Greg has also said that she has Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS) and Mast Cell Activation Syndrome (MCAS). She believed that with the right AI tools, her arduous investigation might have been made much simpler. “Her whole passion for AI is driven by this medical journey,” said her friend and former colleague Sujay Jaswa.

In her late 30s, Anna was also diagnosed with autism. “Her autism can come at a cost, one of which is requiring a lot of alone time (the fur kids and myself excluded) and downtime to rest and recover,” her husband wrote, referring to their many pets. “A beautiful trait of her autism is her deep connection to animals and attention to understanding their needs,” Greg posted on X.

He, too, required patience from his partner while he focused on his interior life. During their first holiday season together, he decided to teach himself machine learning, scratching out equations in a notebook. “She was there with me no matter how many planned activities it meant skipping,” he wrote on his blog. He described her as “someone who made me feel it was ok if I failed.” Greg said on the Tetragrammaton With Rick Rubin podcast that they even put off having children so that he could focus all his energy on AI.

Anna’s early adoption of AI tools helped her practically float up the corporate ladder, but it also opened the door to loftier visions. In a 2018 blog post, she wrote, “I believe in the power of AI to allow us to become more human, today and in the future, by alleviating monotony and opening the space for creativity and intuition.”

Meanwhile, Greg sounded like he was experiencing vertigo from the progress they were making at OpenAI. His journals from this period, portions of which were later made public as part of discovery for the Musk v. Altman trial, ricochet between self-doubt and megalomania. “No person should have control over what we’re creating,” he wrote in August 2017. Then three months later, he appeared to copy and paste a chat with an unknown correspondent into the journal document. “It is better for us to become increasingly kings of this industry,” one of them wrote. “Being the kings of AI is not so bad.”

In Anna, he found the ultimate support system. According to the WSJ, he took the other side of a bet with his then OpenAI colleague (and later Anthropic cofounder) Daniela Amodei, who wagered $100 that Anna was not the one. He won. As Greg put it, they “have been inseparable ever since.”

At the Musk v. Altman trial, Anna was by her husband’s side almost every day. Some observers noted that she held his hand right up to the last second as she walked him to the witness stand. Sources who know the couple described Anna, 38, as “very devoted” and Greg, 38, as “the ultimate wife guy.”

When Anna and Greg got married in 2019, they held a civil ceremony in OpenAI’s office officiated by fellow OpenAI cofounder Ilya Sutskever. The ring bearer was a robotic hand.

As wife to the “wife guy” at the helm of one of the most powerful companies on earth, Anna has enjoyed a front row seat to scenes of such intrigue that they have inspired multiple books, and the highly anticipated upcoming film Artificial. (Cooper Hoffman, the actor who plays Brockman in the film Artificial, recalls director Luca Guadagnino’s guidance on how to approach the role: “Greg is all-American,” Guadagnino told him. “He’s like a cheeseburger.”)

The Brockmans attended the Met Gala in 2025.

While it isn’t uncommon for spouses and partners to turn up in the offices of start-ups, sources who’ve spent time with the Brockmans noted that by the late 2010s Anna was unusually engaged in his work life, having left her own job at the venture capital firm Basis Set Ventures. While, per The Information, Anna has never been formally employed at OpenAI, over the years she has appeared in live product demos; accompanied executives on trips, like one to South Korea to meet with local start-ups; and even been spotted at high-level meetings at the OpenAI office.

When OpenAI’s top executives were appointed drivers and private security, Anna would sometimes be spotted in the car with Greg, taking him to work, according to former colleagues.

As the money piled up, the relationships between the company’s early team—including Sam Altman, Greg Brockman, Ilya Sutskever, Jakub Pachocki, Mira Murati, and Dario and Daniela Amodei—began to fray. While the imaginations of many of their Bay Area peers ran wild with sci-fi visions of uploaded consciousness and unfathomable abundance, and AI doomsayers warned of extinction events, the Brockmans’ hopes for an AI future felt relatively pedestrian.

Greg was firmly in the pro-commercialization camp, according to OpenAI researchers who’ve worked with him, believing that above all, AI can empower individuals to transform their own lives. Anna, meanwhile, is driven by the “idea that AI for all is gonna take all these major social problems, like the extreme cost of health care and education [and] extreme inequality in access…and it’s gonna democratize all of it,” according to Jaswa.

And to do that, the Brockmans understood that AI leaders needed to win over the policymakers that, in their view, could stand in the way of AGI.

Following the release of ChatGPT in 2022, OpenAI’s founding team found themselves on the other side of overnight fame—at least in the insular tech bubble of the Bay Area. While some of the more socially awkward researchers chafed at the attention, Greg—who’d been promoted to president of the company—and Anna have seemed to bask in it.

The Brockmans have dined with Sylvester Stallone at the Kennedy Center, attended black-tie events at the White House, and even walked the blue carpet at the Met Gala, where Anna wore a black-and-white ruffled gown by Korean designer Ashlynn Park.

The power she’d been quietly amassing by Greg’s side played out in a more significant and dramatic way in November 2023, when the board of OpenAI removed Sam Altman from his position as CEO over concerns that he was untrustworthy. Sutskever, who was on the board, also compiled a memo detailing allegations against Greg, and Greg was removed from his position as chairman of the board (but allowed to stay on as president). When the board called Greg to inform him of their decision, the first thing he did was talk to his wife. He told her, “‘We have to leave.’ And she said, ‘Yes, we do,’” he said on the Tetragrammaton With Rick Rubin podcast. He warned her they would have to be prepared for his equity to disappear if he quit. “‘Still want to do it?’ And she said yes.”

But when the board began to reconsider its decision, Sutskever became the deciding vote. In an oft-repeated piece of OpenAI lore, Anna allegedly begged Sutskever in a tearful encounter to reconsider. (Sources familiar with the events have suggested that the impact of this encounter has been overstated.) According to the WSJ, when Sutskever decided to reverse his decision, Anna left him a cactus as a gift.

After a long negotiation over his place at the company, Sutskever left to start his own venture, Safe Superintelligence. “There were some deep and bitter things” that went down during this period, according to one high-level employee at the time.

After this dramatic inflection point, which has come to be known as the blip, Greg took a three-month leave of absence. This period allowed him to dedicate himself to a project he was passionate about: developing a biological foundation model for genome modeling and design at the Arc Institute—“a domain that’s very personally meaningful to both me and and to my wife,” he has said.

Meanwhile, the company had replaced nearly all the board members who’d risen up against Altman with what one former senior OpenAI employee called a “more loyal and ‘normie’” board who were supportive of the company’s commercial push.

The center of gravity began to shift in Greg’s direction, solidifying his place as Altman’s second in command, soon to be tasked with an even more fraught assignment: building political goodwill. What wouldn’t the billionaire couple do to help the technology that they consider vital to humanity’s future?

“He thinks big, but he is also very practical, kind of a realist,” Peter Welinder, OpenAI’s vice president and general manager, says of Greg. Others felt that his techno-optimism, and subsequent push into Washington to defend those ideals, is “naivete,” says the former high-level employee. “I don’t think he’s very carefully thinking through the political and power implications.”

When Donald Trump was reelected in late 2024, OpenAI found itself facing down a new threat. Elon Musk, an original cofounder of the company who left in 2018, had grown increasingly antagonistic toward his onetime colleagues while also growing close to the incoming administration. According to Kevin Roose’s The AGI Chronicles, OpenAI, and Altman in particular, feared political retribution from Musk, who now had his own competitor company in xAI, if he was allowed to take up all the oxygen in Washington. At the same time, OpenAI’s need for energy and compute had grown so insatiable that the company had no choice but to seek the government’s help. In an administration run on quid pro quo, OpenAI would have to make nice.

Brockman found himself uniquely well-positioned to lead the infrastructure-scaling bonanza, thanks to a preexisting relationship with Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum, who hailed from his home state of North Dakota. Greg was also “the most credible” face of the political donations, said one former OpenAI employee.

And so Greg and Anna Brockman became White House mainstays. They have attended state dinners for foreign leaders like Saudi crown prince Mohammed bin Salman and Xi Jinping, and joined top tech executives at a White House event about the future of AI. Brockman, rather than Altman, flanked Trump during the signing of the White House Accord on Super Intelligence in September.

When the political pendulum began to swing back this summer, it began to appear as though whoever had made the call on those political donations might have made a severe miscalculation. Following a steady drumbeat of negative headlines about Leading the Future’s work and significant internal dissent among OpenAI employees, the Brockmans rescinded their second planned $25 million donation to the PAC. Greg wrote in a Slack message, obtained by The New York Times, that Leading the Future had become a “distraction” from OpenAI’s work.

When I reached out to OpenAI to discuss the Brockmans’ political giving, it directed me back to the Brockmans’ team. In an interview this October with Vanity Fair’s global editorial director Mark Guiducci, Altman said, “I did not ask him to donate or stop donating. He can make his own personal decision.” It seems the Brockmans’ donations are a hot potato no one is eager to catch.

Regardless, their $25 million checks have helped provide the funds to enable a torrent of preelection ads, including warnings like, “This is the final battle” to “liberate America from these villains, once and for all.”

Some observers of the company have come to believe that the plan was “to have Greg be the scapegoat if/when the Democrats come back into power, but to allow OpenAI to privately (with the White House) claim credit for the MAGA PAC donations with the Trump administration while privately (with employees) distance itself from them,” according to the former senior employee. (OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment.)

Meanwhile, Greg has returned more of his focus to the product realm, and he and his wife have found a less controversial way to spend their millions. When the couple found out that the Big Bear Valley habitat of two publicly beloved eagles, Jackie and Shadow, was under threat, they donated over $5.5 million to preserve the land this summer. “[Jackie and Shadow] inspire perseverance and a sense of connectedness to something greater,” Anna said of their donation.

“It was clear in talking to her that she loved her husband very much and that she loved the eagles,” says Jenny Voisard, the communications and PR leader for Friends of Big Bear Valley, of her experience working with Anna on the donation. They never talked about politics.

#3693. How To Pitch Stories To Kotaku

We’ve worked with a ton of different freelance writers at Kotaku over the years. Maybe you want to be one of them! Here’s what you need to know before pitching us stories.

The good ones. Especially if you have a unique angle or access to provide our readers with exclusive insights, information, or high-quality writing about something they never knew they wanted to read about before. This includes, but is not limited to, feature stories, opinion pieces, essays, reported scoops, sweeping investigations, and fascinating interviews.

Most of the pitches we get are for reviews and previews. These are also the easiest things to say no to because everyone else will be publishing them. What Kotaku is most interested in when it comes to freelance pitches are original stories that readers won’t be able to find anywhere else because of a unique angle you’ve crafted, insight you’ve unearthed, experience you’ve had, or information you’ve obtained.

This could be an interview with a developer that surfaces a fascinating insight about a game they worked on a decade ago. It could be a bizarre but intriguing drama that played out in a video game Discord community last month. It could be insights from a studio about why a troubled project still hasn’t shipped or a profile of a group of modders attempting something incredible in one of their favorite games.

The best stories inform and entertain. They have characters, conflict, and tension. Some stories have exciting conclusions. Others remain unresolved and are richer because of it. You don’t have to be pitching the next Pulitzer Prize-winning article to be thinking about these types of things.

Send us your idea for what you want to write with a projected word count and timeline for when it would be filed. Suggest a sample headline and explain what makes the story interesting, why we have to have it, and why there’s no version of it that we’ll be able to find online within five minutes of Googling for it. This pitch should be brief, punchy, and as exciting as the final version of the article you’re going to turn in.

Please also share a link to relevant past work and any public profile you maintain. We don’t need to know your entire life’s story or everything you’ve ever written, just one or two strong samples, whether published at a mainstream website or your personal blog, that help demonstrate your ability to execute on the ambitious idea you just pitched us.

Send them to [email protected]. Or you can reach out to individual members of staff. Don’t hesitate to follow up if you don’t get a response right away. And while we can’t guarantee we’ll get back to every pitch, we definitely read them all. We do not accept work produced by AI agents or drafted with the help of them.

Our rates start at $50 for short news posts (300-450 words). Our standard rate for short features (750-1,000 words) is $150. These include light research and some original sourcing (quotes or information revealed for the first time in this story), and often try to show a trend, convey a larger point, or make a broader argument about gaming and the world, although they certainly don’t have to. Sometimes hyper-detailed anecdotes or chains of events within niche communities make for the most interesting reads of all.

We pay up to $300 for more in-depth articles that require multiple interviews, more intensive research, or lots of hands-on time with a game. Rates for everything in-between and beyond are negotiable on a case-by-case basis. If you show up with a leaked build of Half-Life 3 or an exclusive interview with Shigeru Miyamoto, we can talk.

#3692. GOG Wants To Bring Back Physical PC Games, But There’s A Catch

While PlayStation 5 console owners are preparing for a discless future, PC gamers have been living in all-digital world for decades now. The advent of Steam and cheaper broadband internet helped end physical PC game sales in the early 2000s, but GOG is dreaming up a future where these games can thrive once again--if it can get past a few obstacles that stand in its way.

Speaking to GamesRadar, Marcin Paczynski, GOG's senior business development and partnerships manager, laid out a dream scenario in which a consumer can browse GOG, select a game, and have a physical copy delivered to their home. "Ideally, my dream would be to be able to buy physical versions of those games on GOG," Paczynski said. "You go to your shelf on GOG, you click on the game that you would like to receive a physical copy of, you order it, and it gets to you. That would be a perfect scenario."

While that sounds ideal, it's easier said than done, as Paczynski noted that selling physical goods is a logistical challenge when compared to running a digital storefront. Physical media requires organizing storage, delivery, and additional publisher approvals, but Paczynski hopes to see it realized one day.

It's worth noting that the GOG Preservation Program did recently create high-resolution scans for five classic games--Myst, Descent, Hitman: Codename 47, Star Trek: 25th Anniversary, and Armikrog--and turned them into 3D models that you can view on your PC--as well as printable files for anyone looking for a papercraft project. It's similar to the work done by another site, Big Box Collection, which offers a far larger library of classic PC boxes to admire in 3D.

GOG isn't the only company nostalgic for the big boxes of a bygone era; several sites have popped up in recent years to offer curated collections of physical PC and console games. From Limited Run Games to Special Reserve Games, there's still an appetite for owning something with a tangible quality.

A standing ovation from all four coaches turned one The Voice singer into a frontrunner.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Spoiler alert! This story discusses Cut Week on The Voice Season 30, which aired November 2. Episodes are available to stream the day after they air with a Peacock subscription.

Season 30 of NBC’s long-running singing competition The Voice, currently airing on the 2026 TV schedule, is heating up with the first ever Cut Week. Due to audience demand, the Live Shows are back with six weeks of live competition, but before the singers could get to that next step, coaches Kelly Clarkson, Queen Latifah, Adam Levine and Riley Green had to make the biggest elimination in one week ever in the history of the show.

To get into the specifics, Cut Week saw each coach send two artists straight through to the Live Shows while the remaining five had to sing their hearts out as they battled for the last remaining spot. That’s three singers for each coach going through to the next round, with one additional pick made by America to round out the Top 13. While some coaches agonized over who to fill their final slot with, The Voice newbie Riley Green had the easiest selection of the night.

This latest episode breezed by, as five singers for each team, 20 in total, gave everything they had to their performances in the attempt to win their individual coach over. The thing that surprised me the most about this new twist that was replacing the Knockouts, also known as Adam Levine’s least favorite part of the competition, was that each artist sang on a level where any of them were deserving of being sent through to the Live Shows. I’ve got to say, Cut Week was painful, with more than half of each team getting dropped all at once and having to say goodbye to truly talented competitors.

For me, the most shocking decision was the Maroon 5 frontman choosing to let Brandon Diaz, his steal from Team Queen, slip through his fingertips. Not to take anything away from Dakota Cohen’s performance of “Hemorrhage (In My Hands),” which was a worthy rock rendition that had Queen Latifah singing along.

However, Brandon’s version of “Dare You to Move” showcased expertly skilled vocals, and they prove he has what it takes to win. Not only that, but performance also ahd the Equalizer star and American Idol winner giving Brandon a standing ovation. That’s why I couldn’t believe Levine didn’t send him through to the next round.

While Riley Green didn’t get every single country singer on Season 30 for his team, he came pretty close, often pulling out all the stops to get them to choose him as their coach. From the beginning, 19-year-old Joe Henley has been a stand-out, so it was surprising when he didn’t get one of the automatic spots for the Live Shows. But his rendition of the Keith Whitley song “Don’t Close Your Eyes” was so heartfelt from the first note to the last that he earned the only four coach standing ovation of the night.

While the Marshals guest star said he thought he knew he was going to pick before Joe took the stage, Kelly Clarkson declared that she would be mind blown if he didn’t make it to the finale. It made Green’s decision to put Joe Henley through an absolute no-brainer, because he really could end up winning the season.

After the craziness of Cut Week, what I’m most curious about with next week’s episode is to learn who America will pick out of everyone the coaches eliminated. Clearly, I’m rooting for Brandon, but there wasn’t one bad performance from the 16 remaining singers. On that note, we’ll see how that turns out.

While we already know the competition series will be shaking things up with Season 31’s The Voice: Celebrity, we won’t learn who Season 30’s winner will be until December. So, be sure to keep tuning in to NBC on Mondays at 8 p.m. ET until then.

Sony appears to have an exclusive marketing campaign with Rockstar Games for Grand Theft Auto 6. We don’t know what the terms of the deal were, but it has afforded the PlayStation maker all sorts of opportunities to announce things like “GTA 6 will play best on PS5.” The game is obviously also coming to Xbox, but Microsoft isn’t allowed to talk about that in its blog posts, so it stuffed an Xbox Series X inside of an alligator instead.

“Measuring more than five feet from snout to tail, the console sits inside a meticulously crafted alligator, visible through an illuminated Xbox Nexus in its body,” the company announced today. “A custom Xbox Wireless Controller with bite marks rests between its jaws, complete with Xbox-green irises and Nexus-inspired pupils, making the Xbox Series X-BITE ready to play some of the biggest games of the year. The result is part-Xbox Series X, part-creature fabrication.”

The ’80s-style synth-backed teaser for the limited edition Xbox makes the GTA-ness of it all clear despite never mentioning the game:

The X-Bite isn’t being mass produced. The animatronic produced by John Nolan Studio, which has produced similar creatures for shows like The Witcher and movies like Jurassic World Dominion, is completely one-of-a-kind. The only way to obtain it is to win one of the special sweepstakes Xbox still loves doing.

So why pull this stunt? Why put an illuminated Xbox power-on button inside the spiny scales of a five-foot gator? I suppose it was one Xbox marketing person’s clever workaround for the GTA 6 marketing exclusivity deal. “This November, Xbox is heading to Florida,” the blog post reads. Why is Xbox heading to Florida? The post never says. The words “Grand Theft Auto 6,” “Rockstar Games,” and “Vice City” are nowhere to be found.

“Reminds me of companies that want to advertise around the Super Bowl but donât pay up so they have to say ‘The Big Game,'” wrote Giant Bomb cofounder Jeff Gerstmann on Bluesky. “‘Hey, if youâre going to sit down and play Big Florida Crime 6 this month, do it on a gator!'”

GTA 6 will likely play the same on Xbox Series X as it does on PS5, as 99 percent of multiplatform games have this console generation. Even from the inside of an animatronic gator.
