#3689. Borderlands Franchise Hits 100 Million Sales As Gearbox Hints At What’s Next

The Borderlands franchise has reached a new sales milestone, as developer Gearbox Software announced that Borderlands 4 had pushed the series over the 100 million units sold mark. Celebrating the achievement, the studio also took time to reveal what's next for Borderlands 4 as it enters its second year, as well as plans it's busy cooking up for the IP.

"We just wrapped our Year 1 roadmap, and the team is cooking hard on more Borderlands 4 content for next year," Gearbox wrote in a blog post, adding that weekly activity refreshes and Community Challenges will continue in the game. So what's next for Borderlands? Gearbox says that it's "a bigger look at the franchise as a whole," and it's also listening to fans to gauge which characters they want to spend more time with.

Don't expect Gearbox to drop a Borderlands 5 announcement anytime soon, as the developer said it needs time and space to work on future projects. "Big plans take time, and we need some room to work. You can trust that we’ll talk more when the time is right," Gearbox added. Thirteen months ago, Gearbox Software boss Randy Pitchford had predicted that Borderlands 4 would continue to sell millions of copies and would help the franchise cross the 100 million units sold line eventually. "We will break 100 million units with this launch, easily, all in, with the franchise," Pitchford said at the time.

To put that in perspective, the Borderlands franchise had sold 94 million units through August 2025, meaning Borderlands 4 would move at least 6 million copies. Historically, Borderlands 2 is the franchise's top seller, with 31 million units sold, while Borderlands 3 is second with 23 million sales to date. It's worth noting that these games have also gone on sale regularly--with Borderlands 3 once being sold for just $3 on PC via Steam--and Borderlands 4 has also received a few discounts since launch. Gearbox and publisher Take-Two Interactive haven't revealed sales figures for Borderlands 4 yet, so it's hard to know where it currently fits on the Borderlands sales chart.

The game didn't have a smooth launch either, as various technical hurdles required multiple rounds of patching, and the oft-delayed Switch 2 edition was eventually paused so that Gearbox could focus on the PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X|S editions of the game.

#3688. Donald Trump Says He'll Move to Israel and Be New PM If Voters Turn on Him

As millions of Americans head to the polls to cast their vote on Election Day, President Donald Trump is threatening to leave the United States altogether.

“If people ever get tired of me in the U.S., I’ll move to Israel and become prime minister,” the commander-in-chief, 80, claimed while calling into the Tuesday, November 3, episode of Fox & Friends and after touting his alleged popularity in the region.

“I’m at 99 [percent approval,” Trump claimed. “I have the highest approval rating of anybody in history.”

Trump’s apparent plans to leave the U.S. if he is no longer popular with the electorate comes amid the president’s record-low approval ratings. In a new CNN poll taken between October 13 and October 26, Trump’s disapproval rating in the United States was at 64 percent.

The president’s overall approval rating dropped to 34 percent. Just nine states still rate Trump positively, including Wyoming, North Dakota and Arkansas.

The president’s comments also come after he claimed the United States will no longer be sending military aid to Israel. (The U.S. sends approximately $4 billion in military aid to the country every year.)

“Israel’s our No. 1. We give them more than anybody else, and they no longer need it,” Trump said via phone during the on-air interview. “We’ve been doing it for years. I’ve been doing it. But Israel is a very thriving country. They don’t need it. If they did need it, I would say keep it going.”

Trump claimed to have recently made a deal with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for the United States to stop funding the country’s military, including the country’s missile-defense system the Iron Dome. The president alleged the pair “made a deal months ago” and that the money would get “cut off at the end of the year.”

“They’ve been a great partner, but we stopped Iran,” he said before changing topics drastically. “Iran was an unstoppable force. We knocked the hell out of them.”

Netanyahu, 77, has yet to publicly comment on the president’s claims.

Trump’s interview comes during a pivotal midterm election for the United States. Depending on the results in several key states, Democrats could take back control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives as Trump continues his second presidential term.

Hours before voting centers closed on the East Coast, Trump said he was watching Fox News and didn’t approve of one of the guests speaking.

“Watching the Pre-Election Results on Fox News, but I can’t stand Jessica Tarlov‘s voice — DUMB AS A ROCK, but it’s the voice that gets me,” he wrote via Truth Social on Tuesday. “Have to go somewhere else until that LOSER is off the air — I’ll be back later!”

#3687. Ta-Nehisi Coates on Haley Stevens, Abdul El-Sayed, and the Right’s “Campaign of Hate”

When Michigan congresswoman Haley Stevens endorsed Republican Mike Rogers yesterday, she offered a curious framing. “I’m choosing country over hate,” Stevens claimed. “This is not anti-Muslim at all.”

Rogers, for his part, invoked Martin Luther King Jr.: “You cannot solve darkness with darkness; you have to solve it with light. You can’t solve hate with hate; you have to solve it with love.” For the site of their hard launch, the odd couple chose Perfecting Church, a Black church in Detroit, evidently seeking to exploit the aura of social justice implicit in the Black faith tradition.

Aura farming aside, it is very hard to square the claims of patriotism and love with the actual campaign that Stevens now supports. Indeed, since the moment Abdul El-Sayed triumphed in the Democratic Senate primary, Rogers has made his views of his opponent clear. “I spent years hunting terrorists and bringing Osama bin Laden to justice,” he claimed the morning after El-Sayed won. “Never in a million years did I think that I would be running against someone who believes America deserved 9/11.” (Never mind that Hasan Piker, not El-Sayed, said the 9/11 quote, which El-Sayed has disavowed.)

Indeed, a consistent theme of Rogers’s campaign has been the implication that El-Sayed is a tool for shadowy forces originating in the East. “The Muslim Brotherhood celebrated exactly one victory in the United States in the primary this year,” Rogers claimed. “Abdul El-Sayed’s.” As a factual matter, the attack is highly dubious. But facts are not the point, so much as the deployment of “Muslim” as a slur.

To understand this, one need only look to the overlord of the Rogers campaign, President Donald Trump. As is his wont, Trump delights in mangling El-Sayed’s name, referring to him as “Abduladadalalalala” or simply “Mohamed.” “Somebody said his name isn’t Mohamed,” Trump told attendees at a rally. “I’m the president, I can call him whatever the hell I want. To me, he’s Mohamed.”

The Trump theory of El-Sayed holds that his ascendance is being facilitated by the machinations of Wayne County, a “strictly Third World” jurisdiction that seeks to elevate to Congress a “jihadist” who shouldn’t even be eligible for “a seat on an airplane.” If seated in the world’s greatest deliberative body, El-Sayed, the theory holds, would execute his dastardly plan to ban Christmas and—you guessed it—impose Sharia law.

Trump’s attacks have been echoed and amplified by right-wing news outlets like Newsmax, which has lambasted El-Sayed as an “anti-Israel Muslim,” an “immigrant from another Muslim country,” and a Midwest variant of that other alien, Zohran Mamdani, the “socialist Muslim who’s always smiling.” For those too dense to catch the message, the Newsmax chyrons have helpfully driven home the point—“THE LEFT IS FORGETTING THE HEINOUS ATTACKS OF 9/11,” “DEMOCRATS DROOL OVER NON-WHITE SOCIALISTS,” “MUSLIMS TELL US THEY’RE TAKING OVER, AND THEY ARE.”

Lest one think that this bigotry is merely limited to the crude ramblings of unlettered ogres, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has stepped in to offer some intellectual heft to the attack. The Muslim Brotherhood, according to Kennedy, is responsible for not just the menace that is El-Sayed, but also the dark age that has fallen over the entirety of the Arabdom. “There’s 500 million Arabs in the world,” Kennedy claimed, “and yet they don’t produce science, they don’t win the Nobel Prize, they don’t win the Field[s] prize, they don’t win the Wolf Prize, they don’t produce the literature they used to produce.”

Again, facts aren’t really the point here, and there is no wisdom in debating a quack whose brain has literally been infected by a worm. Nonetheless, it is worth noting the particular history at work. During both his run for president and his time in the White House, Barack Obama endured his share of racist attacks. To Rush Limbaugh, Obama was “Barack the Magic Negro.” To Newt Gingrich, he was America’s “food stamp president.” At the Value Voters Summit, a vendor hawked “Obama Waffles,” a product featuring a racist caricature of the president on the packaging. The tagline was: “Point box toward Mecca for tastier waffles.” That last line deserves particular attention. Indeed, by 2016, the political scientist Philip Klinkner would find that the best way to discern whom a voter would support in the upcoming election was to pose a simple question—“Is Barack Obama a Muslim?”

Stevens, in joining Rogers, has allied herself with this odious culture war, one that is itself tied to a very real war. The campaign of hate, of which El-Sayed is the latest victim, has a simple goal: to render Muslims and Arabs more killable. The latter does not require the former. In 1953 the CIA backed a coup that overthrew a democracy in Iran. In 1965 it supported a coup in Indonesia, the country with the largest Muslim population in the world, that killed between 500,000 and a million people. During the Cold War, the justification for this death toll was the threat of communism; post-9/11, it is racism. In 2008, John McCain confronted a supporter and disputed the claim that Obama was Arab. “No, ma’am,” McCain told his supporter. “He’s a decent family man.” This moment is often referenced as an act of patriotism, and perhaps it was one. But the notion that “decent” people exist in one place, while Arabs exist in another, is the major premise for a syllogism of violent, chauvinist power—wedding parties droned, governments overthrown, schoolgirls bombed, and inconvenient people eliminated.

This long war on the Muslim and Arab world has reached its apogee in the concentration camp of Gaza, where every single bomb was dropped from a plane of American extraction. And the genocide is but the latest chapter in a book authored by Israel, a state whose own basic laws reserve full rights for its “decent” people and something less for everyone else. This is the state that Haley Stevens has claimed to literally see in her dreams. And it is ultimately the defense of this state that drove Stevens into the arms of Mike Rogers. From this perspective, Stevens’s defection isn’t a story about party intrigue. It is a story about Stevens waking up and choosing violence.

#3686. Remedy’s Big Bet On Control Resonant Appears To Be Paying Off

Following the September release of Control Resonant, business is boomin' for developer Remedy Entertainment. The studio reported that its third-quarter revenue surged 226% to €39.6 million / $44.3 million after the game's release, following the financial review period on October 15, a feat CEO Jean-Charles Gaudechon called "a defining milestone" for Remedy.

In terms of operating profit, Remedy said it made €0.6 million / $670,794, and while that may not sound like much, it's still better than the €16.4 million / $18.3 million loss the studio posted in the same quarter last year. Control Resonant has sold over 1 million units, making it Remedy's fastest-selling title to date, with most sales coming from the US. The game has also been popular in the US and the UK, and Remedy says that half of the players were new to the franchise.

"Reaching new players was a key goal for this game, and these early results indicate a growing audience for the franchise and for Remedy," Gaudechon said, adding that the developer is looking to get the game into the hands of more people. Control Resonant's predecessor, Control, also saw increased sales, and that financial runway will help Remedy as it continues working on other projects, like its Max Payne 1 & 2 remake. Gaudechon also noted that Control Resonant is currently on 2.4 million wishlists, which could provide a "substantial potential audience" for the future.

"Excellent player reviews, penetration in all our target markets and a substantial outstanding wishlist base give a solid foundation for the game’s longer-term sales potential, supported by both organic visibility as well as our targeted marketing activities," said Gaudechon. As for the other games in the Remedy catalog, Gaudechon said that most people are playing FBC: Firebreak through subscription services like Game Pass or PlayStation Plus, and in its second year, it is making less money. The Alan Wake franchise had a quieter quarter, but the Alan Wake 2 capitalized development costs were fully depreciated during Q3.

For more on Control Resonant, read up on how different it is from its predecessor, why you have to watch out for scary buses, and the cool little details lurking in the background.

I’ve been thriving off Marvel nostalgia thanks to repeated trips back to the age of Iron Man. First with VisionQuest, and now with some hilarious trivia. I’m always up for some fun BTS stories about the shared universe, but even I couldn’t have predicted how the MCU connects to spy guinea pigs. Yes, you read that correctly. So imagine my reaction when I heard the wild (guinea pig-related) story behind Jon Favreau casting one star for Iron Man 2.

Turns out, we have a family-friendly spy movie to thank for Sam Rockwell’s role as Justin Hammer. For those of you who don’t remember (or hasn’t strayed from the MCU re-watch list for Doomsday), back in 2010 Tony Stark dealt with two villains: Ivan Vanko (played by Mickey Rourke) and Hammer who was Vanko’s benefactor in his crusade against Iron Man. While the second movie doesn’t get as much love, it’s clear that the Galaxy Quest actor enjoyed playing the cheeky bad guy, and even has a connection to Justin Theroux who penned the script. He dished to Esquire on the unique way he landed the part while sharing BTS stories behind some of his popular roles:

Justin and I were friends, and I was dating Leslie Bibb and she had done the first Iron Man. And I went over to Theroux’s apartment just to get coffee, and he's packing a bag. And I'm like, ‘Where are you going?’ He's [like,] ‘I'm going to LA. I'm going to write Iron Man 2.’ I'm like, ‘Get the fuck out of here. I want to be in that. What's the part?’ said, ‘I want to be the bad guy. Let me be the bad guy.’ And he goes, ‘Yeah, yeah, OK, whatever.’

While he’s not involved in any upcoming Marvel projects, I’m glad he got to live out his dream. Not only did he get a part in the movie, he also got to play a bad guy. Justin Hammer has everything you love about Bond villains (plus Sam Rockwell’s cheekiness), and was the perfect charismatic foil to play off of Robert Downey Jr. Though what exactly do guinea pigs have to do with him landing the role? Well, Rockwell explains:

And then, like, six months later, a few months later, I’m doing G-Force, and Jon Favreau and I are in a room playing guinea pigs, and we’re like wrestling around with each other in the sound studio, and he says, ‘Hey, there’s this thing Theroux’s writing.’ I said, ‘Oh, is it Iron Man?’ So he said, ‘I got the Marvel guy coming. We're going to take the villain. We're going to split it in two and we're going to make one the fast talking guy and then sort of alpha. So they got me and Mickey to sort of do both do the villain sort of as two parts.

I shouldn’t be surprised by this story and yet I didn’t expect the two to connect while pretending to be guinea pigs. Am I the only one who can’t stop picturing Happy and Hammer running around pretending to be adorable rodents? Though Favreau has a gift when it comes to picking actors, as he ignored the pushback against RDJ and chose to back him as Iron Man anyway. At the time, he explained that he “just saw it” regarding RDJ in what would be his most famous role. Clearly something about Rockwell’s performance as Darwin (the no-nonsense leader of G-Force) that was perfect to play Hammer.

The actor gave a shout out to a memorable moment. Before you guess, it’s not when he’s fine-dining while interviewing Vanko. Turns out, when Hammer gave the gun demonstration, the actor had to use an earwig as they changed up the props right before filming. What apparently stood out most in the interview was Rockwell’s willingness to return to the MCU if asked. He’s just waiting to get the call. Although Hammer’s return would be the least surprising thing after VisionQuest Episode 6 blasted us back to 2008 with Faran Tahir reprising his Iron Man 1 character. Somehow I missed that casting news prior to watching.

At this point, Justin Hammer could easily come out of the wood works, and I wouldn’t be shocked to learn that he escaped from prison. This would be relatively simple to achieve, especially since our characters keep making trips to the island of Madripoor and it’d be believable that he’d hide out there. Plus, Tony’s rival would easily fit in with the lawless chaos.

So why not include a Benefactor that can face off against the Power Broker?

#3684. Ubisoft Among Those Bidding On Marvel’s Blade Studio Arkane

Months after Microsoft announced that Arkane, maker of Dishonored and Deathloop, would be among the studios it is divesting as part of Xbox’s current “reset,” the tech giant still hasn’t been able to settle on a buyer. Ubisoft is among the companies currently interested in buying the studio and potentially helping it complete work on Marvel’s Blade.

According to a new report by Bloomberg, the Assassin’s Creed publisher is among those currently in talks for a potential deal, having already submitted a bid. Microsoft is also reportedly exploring a sale of the studio back to its management. If no deal can be reached, a total studio closure is on the table. The terms of the proposals are unknown.

A spokesperson for Microsoft told Bloomberg it continues to explore options ahead of a December deadline for a decision.

Ubisoft and Arkane are both based in France, and it wouldn’t be the first time the publisher has worked on a Disney-owned license. It released Star Wars Outlaws in 2024, a game that seemingly failed to meet sales expectations despite being generally quite good.

The French publisher is facing its own headwinds, however. Ubisoft has seen ongoing layoffs and restructurings as it deals with revenue shortfalls and debt payments following big production delays. Despite employing over 15,000 people, it has no major blockbuster releases coming out this fall.

Last month, Microsoft revealed it had extended Arkane’s deadline for finding a potential buyer.

#3683. Jessa Duggar Praises 'Angel' Mom Michelle Duggar's Role as Grandparent

Pregnant Jessa Duggar is happy to give mom Michelle Duggar her flowers as she prepares to welcome baby No. 7.

“Every time that we’ve had a baby, she’s there at the hospital helping us through,” Jessa, 33, said of her mother, 60, during the Wednesday, October 28, episode of the “Unplanned Podcast” hosted by Matt and Abby Howard. “She’s just a calming presence. She’s an angel.”

Michelle, who has 45 grandchildren and counting, has been “the hugest blessing” for Jessa as she raises her six kids alongside husband Ben Seewald.

According to Jessa, her mom is the key to her postpartum recovery after delivering each and every baby.

“My postpartum pregnancy and labor secret is — my mom is an angel,” she shared, calling both Michelle and her dad, Jim Bob Duggar, “the best.”

Jessa said her mom’s help specifically, whether it’s staying up all night with her newborns or cooking and cleaning in those early days, contributes “so much to just how easy it is to recover.”

“She was like, ‘You do not look well. You go home, get a shower, get some sleep in your own bed. I’m here. I’ve got this,'” Jessa said, recalling a moment during her sixth pregnancy when her husband, 31, clearly needed a break. “I was like, ‘Go, babe!’ I know my mom’s got this.”

Seewald added, “She’s the one carrying this child. … If she wants to have another one, wants to be a mom again, who am I to stand in the way of that?”

#3682. South Of Midnight Director Says He Would Not Have Funded The Game

Xbox funded and published 2025's South of Midnight, a highly acclaimed action-adventure game set in the American Deep South. The game's creative director, David Sears, said he believes South of Midnight is a "generational" game that he hopes people discover and play for a long time and one that he thought would help elevate the "prestige" of Xbox.

At the same time, Sears said he wasn't sure Microsoft's spending spree under the previous leaders Phil Spencer and Sarah Bond--which is how Sears' studio Compulsion got the funding to make South of Midnight--was going to work out long term.

"I literally told people, I was like, 'Yeah, wow, this could be terrible.' Because somebody is going to say, someday, 'The money tap ... we're closing those floodgates.' And that's going to have really traumatic results downstream," he told Ben Hanson on MinnMax.

Microsoft spent billions and billions of dollars to buy studios and franchises to help get Xbox Game Pass off the ground. The bet did not work out, and now Spencer and Bond are out. The new Xbox CEO is Asha Sharma, and one of her first moves was to cut costs dramatically with layoffs, studio divestures--including Compulsion--and game cancellations. Sharma also talked about how Game Pass needs to evolve into something that's "more enticing to a broader range of customers.”

Asked directly if he had been in control of the Xbox funding at the time, would Sears have stopped writing checks for games like South of Midnight? "Yeah, probably," he answered (via Kotaku).

"I wanted to make it. No doubt. Obviously. Because we made it. Would I have turned off someone else’s money flow before South of Midnight? Yeah. Because I’m not completely selfless. It just seems like, in hindsight at least, it was unsustainable," Sears said.

A lot of people said Microsoft's spending on Xbox Game Pass was unsustainable and ultimately going to lead to pain and turmoil. Raphael Colantonio, the co-founder of Arkane, said Game Pass is unsustainable and "increasingly damaging" to the industry. Game Pass has been propped up by Microsoft's "infinite money," Colantonio said.

Raccoon Logic studio head Alex Hutchinson spoke out about Game Pass devaluing games earlier this year after his game Revenge of the Savage Planet was a day-one title on Xbox Game Pass. Conversely, Rebellion touted the launch of Atomfall on Game Pass as a huge success for the company.

With Microsoft's big bets not panning out in the way the company envisioned, the Xbox business struggled, and the ensuing Xbox "reset" has been painful for the people, teams, and fans of Xbox. Sears said hindsight is 20/20, but he always had a feeling that things just weren't right and that the bottom could fall out one day in terms of Xbox's spending spree.

"Of course it was going to have a 'shocking' outcome. It’s easy to dissect it now. But at the time ... I would talk to other directors and [they’d] be like, 'How is this happening? How did we get so lucky? Is this a golden era?' And I would always be like ... 'For now,'" he said. "And there’s always a night when Rome burns. I didn’t know exactly when it would be, but I was always worried about it."

Sears went on to say the Microsoft of today is "much more humane" than the company was in the '90s and 2000s, something he said is "remarkable and commendable."

Sears said it's a good thing that Microsoft is allowing studios it wants to let go of get spun out instead of shutting them down outright. Compulsion, for its part, was among the studios that got spun out, and is now operating independently and seeking new projects and funding sources.

South of Midnight originally launched for Xbox and PC in April 2025, later coming to PS5 and Switch 2 in March 2026. Now that Compulsion is independent, buying the game supports the studio directly, and not Xbox.

Throughout all of the downturns at Xbox, Microsoft continues to make gigantic sums of money, in part because Xbox represents just a tiny sliver of the company's overall business. For the latest quarter, Microsoft made $92.3 billion in revenue (up 19%) and a profit of $36.6 billion (up 32%). Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has praised Sharma for gutting the Xbox business so heavily.

#3680. Even Pierce Brosnan Is “Eagerly” Awaiting News of the Next James Bond

Like the rest of us, Pierce Brosnan has been following the seemingly endless and exhaustive search for the next James Bond. Having played 007 across four films, Brosnan says he admires all the actors in the running, but Callum Turner, who played his angsty Manhattanite son in The Only Living Boy in New York, gets a particularly warm mention. “Callum is someone I’ve worked with, and he’s so strong,” Brosnan tells Vanity Fair. As for Dune director Denis Villeneuve’s vision for the franchise, Brosnan is already sold. “I think we are going to be blown away.”

Away from Hollywood, the Irish actor stars in Burberry’s new holiday campaign, celebrating 170 years of the luxury fashion house, alongside actor Fiona Shaw, his son Dylan Thomas Brosnan, and a cast of characters including Dwyane Wade, Cara Delevingne, Gabrielle Union, Nico Parker, and more. Set at the cinematic Longleat House in Wiltshire, England, it’s a festive British Christmas, complete with Burberry’s signature checks and partygoers draped in classic garments. On set, Brosnan found a kindred spirit in Shaw. The two bonded over their shared love of art—though he wishes they had much more time to chat, “It was all too brief with Fiona,” he muses.

Pierce Brosnan in the Burberry Festive 2026 Campaign video.

Pierce Brosnan and Fiona Shaw in the Burberry Festive 2026 Campaign video.

Brosnan is no stranger to good style. Having spent a career playing some of the most impeccably dressed men on screen, from James Bond to Thomas Crown, Brosnan has come to re-embrace the joys of good tailoring after an era of rebelling against the gentlemanly image he created for himself. Now, he’s looking forward to seeing a new generation of leading men step into some of those familiar roles, including Michael B. Jordan, whose upcoming take on Thomas Crown he’s cheering on.

In conversation with Vanity Fair, the former 007 talks favorite Christmas traditions, the Burberry Mac he’s kept for years, the art of playing it cool, how filming MobLand shaped his personal style, and the paintings waiting for him in London.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Vanity Fair: The new Burberry campaign celebrates 170 years of the fashion house with a festive Christmas party in the English countryside. How was your time on the campaign set?

Pierce Brosnan: I was with my son, Dylan Thomas Brosnan, which was just absolutely wonderful, and we had the most magnificent time. I’d never seen so many people on a set in all my days for such an event. Everybody was very charming.

Do you typically go all-in on Christmas? What’s your favorite holiday tradition?

I think it starts with the Christmas tree, and my wife really decks the halls, as it were. She loves decorating the tree, and that becomes a great ritual. The boys are much older now, but we do have grandchildren joining us for Christmas. My son Sean Brosnan and his family will be coming down. My wife is a wonderful cook; she’ll make a feast for us all.

Midnight Mass is a tradition and a great joy if we’re in London. Friends, family, and reflection on the year past. Having been brought up within the Catholic religion, the season and all of those traditions are very much ingrained in me.

Harmony Korine (Gummo, Kids, Spring Breakers) directing a holiday campaign feels like such an inspired choice, given how experimental his films can be. What was it like working with him?

I thought he was charming! Very charming. It moved very fast. He was busy and deep in the workload of the day. The highlight was meeting and being with Fiona Shaw. That was just absolutely magnificent. I’m such a huge fan of the lady’s work.

The Burberry trench is such a cornerstone of British style. Is there a clothing item in your wardrobe that holds that kind of status for you?

Oh, dear. There are so many beautiful items in my closet. One of my favorite suits has become a workhorse because it’s so durable. The cloth is wool, and it’s just a two-piece, beautifully tailored suit by Anglo-Italian. I’m very partial to my shoes and belts by Bottega Veneta. And of course, a Burberry Mac, which I’ve had for many, many years. It is the classic, dream trench coat of anyone who has grown up on the movies.

It was wonderful to celebrate such a garment of classic time, and to be in the company of Fiona Shaw. [She’s] someone who I would adore to work with again on any level, really. We had a wonderful time talking about art. We’re both painters, and art is very much part of the tapestry of our lives now.

Pierce Brosnan in The Thomas Crown Affair, 1999.

Speaking of art, I wanted to ask you about playing Thomas Crown in The Thomas Crown Affair. Michael B. Jordan is stepping into that role now, in a new version of the film, which he’s also directing.

I love Michael B. Jordan. I think he’s an outstanding actor and artist, and I wish him every great success with his vision of Thomas Crown. There’s something just beautifully cinematic about the character. He was brought onto the stage by one of the great actors, Steve McQueen, who was so gifted in the art of film acting, stillness, and inner life. For me, the romance with the film came from his body of work as an actor and has always been with me since I was a young lad in Ireland. These characters are very hard to really understand, but they create a sensation.

He was so cool, Steve McQueen. How do you play cool? You play it with sincerity. You play it with stillness, with just the knowingness—and hopefully some humanity and humility, and a kind of inner knowing of being the actor you are.

What do you think makes Thomas Crown such an enduring character?

When I made my rendition and produced it with my late dear friend Beau St. Clair, I wanted to steal art. I didn’t want to steal diamonds or money. I wanted to steal paintings. It was against all the political correctness of his time and space. Thomas Crown was a man who had everything in life: wealth, fortune, intellect. But he didn’t have love. So it was a love story for me.

When we were looking for the film’s art, I suggested René Magritte: the bowler hats, the red tie, the great coat. Magritte is someone I find spellbinding, captivating, and always has a narrative which is almost cinematic. So that’s where the bowler hats came from. The visible and the invisible: Visible with an apple in front of a face, but you don’t see the face. And I thought that translated well to the enigma of Thomas Crown.

Pierce Brosnan and Callum Turner, The Only Living Boy In New York, 2017.

Having played James Bond yourself, I’m curious how you’re following the conversation around this upcoming chapter.

[Laughs.] Oh, I’m just an audience member now. I’m just the man in the street who is eager to see who is going to play this epic role of cinematic history. All the men who are on the list now are actors I admire. Callum, Callum Turner is someone I’ve worked with, and he’s so strong. They all have a voice and a physique, and a presence on film. They all have longevity as actors, all of these young men.

Pierce Brosnan as 007 in The World Is Not Enough, 1999.

What would you say to the next actor stepping into 007?

Whoever plays the role, I wish him the very best of life and strength and courage. You know, it’s hard to tell who it would be, but I eagerly await to hear the news and the celebration of the next James Bond.

Martin Campbell gave your era such a memorable introduction with GoldenEye. Now, with Denis Villeneuve taking on the franchise, what are you most curious to see him bring to Bond?

I think we are going to be blown away. I really do. [Villeneuve] is such an iconoclastic director. His work is visionary, and his stealth and imagination of camera work and storytelling is so visceral and sensuous. It’s going to be great. It’s going to be truly magnificent. Of course, we all get sentimental and nostalgic, and you have to give it time and be patient, and it’s always such a delightful game. But Villeneuve is someone who I have great admiration for, and I look forward to seeing the work.

Pierce Brosnan as Remington Steele, 1986.

Pierce Brosnan as Remington Steele, 1986.

You’ve played some of cinema’s most impeccably dressed men! Have those characters influenced the way you dress in your own life?

I have always been, I suppose, a clothes horse. When I played Remington Steele, I delved into the work of Cary Grant, another emblem of cinema that I’ve admired. Bob Butler, who directed it, said, “We’re making an old movie,” so I styled myself and had the joy of wearing beautiful suits every week. That continues through my life.

As I’ve gotten older, I used to try to rebel against the look, character, and style of actor I had created for myself. Now I embrace it more because it excites me. I love the elegance of tailored clothes and dressing up, and fitting into the season, the gale of emotion, the world around you.

You’ve got some great hunting coats in MobLand too.

Rebecca Hale, the costume designer, has brought so many great ingredients to the world of Conrad. He’s an Irishman from a hard part of Irish life, the Troubles, a mangled life of abuse and violence. He wants to fit into the world of the Cotswolds and be the gentleman. There’s this magnificent coat in MobLand, where Conrad has a shootout, and they made a magnificent overcoat, which I managed to keep from last season. And, of course, I step back and just revel at what Dame Helen Mirren does. She is such an empress of fashion herself.

When Vanity Fair last caught up with you, around your first solo exhibition, you’d already been painting and curating work for years. How has your relationship with art evolved since then?

I had, yes. I had the exhibition three years ago, and it was a great success in the sense that I had the courage to step out and show the work. I have a body of work now that has progressed, and hopefully I will have another showing here, maybe in London.

Do you find that painting gives you something different from acting, or do the two creative practices feed into each other?

Both are essential to my life. Acting is how I make my living and provide for my family. And to be able to have a lifestyle that is not only creative but productive, and then is hopefully entertaining, because you’re working towards an audience.

The practice of my art is a constant exploration of inner life, inner thoughts, inner emotions expressed through color and form. Having lived in Kauai for 25 years, there’s a wonderful artist there who’s become my teacher, Saim Caglayan. Both are necessary to my life. They soothe me and frustrate me and challenge me and exhilarate me—sometimes all in the same space of day and time.

Yes! I was sketching when I was doing Burberry. There was a lovely landscape down there, and I have my sketchbook with me at all times. I wanted so much to be an artist, to be a writer, a poet, to live a creative life. I have no real head for figures or the abstraction of figures, but I certainly have a great love for art and the power of art on the wall.

With the holidays coming up, and hopefully a little time to slow down, is there anything you’re hoping to make more time for, creatively or personally?

I have a little time left before I go back to London with my wife, Keely. London is home, and my mother of 94 is there, so I’m looking forward to seeing her. In my studio, I have a number of paintings that I’m quite pleased with, and I’d like to finish a couple more. And I’m really excited to jump into season three of MobLand. I have no idea where the story is going. Conrad is slowly, slowly going bonkers. But the thing is, he’s aware of it, and the love story of Maeve and Conrad lives on. It’s very exciting.

#3679. Buying GTA 6 Could Save You $5,000, Or At Least This Guy Thinks So

Self-made millionaire Mark Tilbury has shared some advice for how buying GTA 6 can actually save you $5,000. Just don't take this too seriously.

Here's how he arrived at that number: If the game costs $100 (for the Ultimate Edition) and it takes 80 hours to complete, that works out to $1.25/hour of "fun." After adding on side missions and simply exploring GTA 6's map, investing in the game seems like an even better deal at just 50 cents of fun per hour.

If you play for four hours every evening, that's 50 nights of entertainment. Tilbury said people should compare this to a night out where they could easily spend $100 in a night.

"That's why buying GTA 6 actually saves you $5,000," Tilbury says.

Even if it's not a full $100, Tilbury is spot-on that going out to do most things today costs a pretty penny. So staying in to play GTA 6 may indeed "save" you some money you might have spent elsewhere. You may also play a lot of GTA 6 and continue to go out and spend money on other things.

His math also might be conservative, as people are no doubt going to play GTA 6 for far more than 50 days, especially when GTA Online 2.0 releases in 2027, as expected.

Clearly, though, Tilbury is being cheeky here and created the clip for virality and for people to send to their friends and partners to justify how much they are going to play GTA 6.

GTA 6 launches on November 19 for PS5 and Xbox Series X|S, and a PC edition is expected to be released in 2027.

#3678. Hilary Duff Reveals Her 'Spicy' Revenge on a Boy Who Was Mean to Her Friend

If you mess with Hilary Duff’s friends, you’ll evidently pay for it.

“This guy was doing my friend real dirty and we were hitting the bottle,” Duff, 39, revealed in an interview with Billboard published on Tuesday, November 3. “We were spicy and we went and bought the cheapest, grossest can of wieners and tuna and we just had a little field day on his front lawn.”

Although the “Come Clean” singer didn’t name the slighted friend, she did expand on what her girls’ nights would often entail before she had children.

“I’m, like, spicy, so my spicy nights [are] kind of evil,” she explained, adding that the prank occurred during her “late teen-hood.”

Duff shares three daughters — Banks, 8, Mae, 5, and Townes, 2 — with her husband, Matthew Koma, as well as son Luca, 14, with her ex Mike Comrie.

Her comments come after recently jetting away to Mexico with a group of friends for some downtime, including Mandy Moore, What’s Cooking Gabby author Gaby Dalkin, makeup artist Kelsey Deenihan Fisher, skincare professional Whitney Wagner Hartley, artist Amanda Lillywhite, Better Babies founder Janice Gott and influencer Haylee Christine.

“The group chat made it to the jungle,” the actress captioned an October 10 Instagram carousel that showed the celebrity mom friends lapping up luxury throughout One&Only Mandarina resort, which is located in the coastal rainforest of Mexico’s Riviera Nayarit.

In several snaps, Duff was seen rocking a high-cut yellow one-piece, going between sipping on coconuts by the water and playing mahjong with her friends.

The girls’ getaway comes less than a year after a former member of Duff’s mom group, Ashley Tisdale French, penned an essay for New York Magazine’s The Cut titled “Breaking Up With My Toxic Mom Group.” (Tisdale French, 41, shares daughters Jupiter, 5, and Emerson, 2, with husband Christopher French.)

The essay attracted headlines after Tisdale French alleged that she felt “frozen out” of the mom group and wasn’t invited to multiple get togethers.

“I told myself it was all in my head, and it wasn’t a big deal,” she wrote in January. “And yet, I could sense a growing distance between me and the other members of the group.”

While Tisdale French did not name anybody in the essay, social media users speculated that Duff and Moore, 42, were among the moms she had referred to.

Duff later addressed the drama during an appearance on the “Call Her Daddy” podcast. “It sucks to read something that’s not true, and it sucks on behalf of six women and all of their lives,” the singer told host Alex Cooper during the February 25 episode. “I felt really sad. I honestly felt really sad. I was pretty, pretty taken aback and felt just sad.”

The Scene In You Can See Everything That Showed EVERYTHING Might NOT Have Been Billy Evans' Idea

I Wondered Why Nathan Fielder Was Picked For You Can See Everything. His Answer Confused Me

I'm Shocked To Learn One Surprising Scene In You Can See Everything Came From Billy Evans Himself

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In the weeks since You Can See Everything hit the 2026 movie schedule and started tearing up the box office, it's no surprise that some of those tickets have been sold to former Theranos employees. Whistleblower Tyler Schultz spoke out shortly after the Nathan Fielder/Lance Oppenheim-directed documentary about the company’s founder, Elizabeth Holmes, was released, and now more employees are speaking out about their takeaways from the movie. Two of them recently spoke to The Times about it. Here’s what they have to say.

According to the article, former Theranos creative director Gage Clegg and former chief creative officer Patrick O’Neill saw the movie together, and they described their complicated feelings to the paper. O’Neill is glad that people are finally seeing the real Holmes, in his estimation, telling the paper:

No one’s asking me any more how I could possibly work for someone like that; people now understand it … I’m excited that the world is going to experience Elizabeth in the way that I did. People will finally understand her ability to persuade and to connect, and how that gave her such enormous power. [Fielder] fell for it, too.

Much has been said of Holmes’ ability to manipulate people, and some have said Fielder fell under her spell while living with her and her partner, Billy Evans, while he and Oppenheim shot the movie. Personally, I’m not sure he did, but it's easy to see how people fall for it when watching You Can See Everything. Clegg was more direct, saying the documentary:

Sees her as being kind of on the spectrum, a person who doesn’t understand regular people, as a way to garner sympathy and to make people think that maybe she didn’t really understand that what she was doing was wrong. That is crazy. The person I knew was smart, capable and decisive. She walked into the room and owned the room. She is a night and day different person from who was in Fielder’s movie.

As to whether or not they think people should believe the Holmes they saw in the movie, Clegg’s answer was clear: No. He told the paper:

Hearing her say that she didn’t know she was lying made me want to jump out of my seat in the cinema.

Clegg and O’Neill were not alone in pointing out both the deception and the role-playing they see in Holmes. A former in-house lawyer for Theranos (yikes!), Brad Arington, summed up seeing the movie the same way.

She’s always performing. She’s very convincing. I wasn’t going to fall for it again.

Whether or not Fielder fell under Holmes’ spell is one of the big questions the movie leaves audiences wondering. It’s even brought up in the movie itself when he is questioned by another star in the movie over whether he’d gotten too close to his subject.

In fact, the last scene in the movie, with Fielder and Holmes swimming together in the ocean, harkens back to an earlier scene when Holmes tried to convince Fielder to go on a swim with her. Fielder demurs, saying he doesn’t want to, but obviously did swim with her at some point. Was that Fielder reinforcing the notion that Holmes can sell anything to anyone? The film doesn’t answer that for us.

Like so much in the movie, we’re really just stuck asking more questions than getting answers, and for me, that is part of what makes the movie an Oscar contender, and one of the best movies of the year.

Hugh Scott is the Syndication Editor for CinemaBlend. Before CinemaBlend, he was the managing editor for Suggest.com and Gossipcop.com, covering celebrity news and debunking false gossip. #3676. Final Fantasy 7 Remake And Rebirth Are Absurdly Cheap On Switch 2 Right Now

Final Fantasy VII RebirthFinal Fantasy VII RemakeSaleSwitch 2

Final Fantasy VII Remake Intergrade and Rebirth both came to Switch 2 earlier this year and they are currently just $8 each. That is a ridiculously low price for two very good ports of two excellent RPGs.

Rebirth is normally $50 and Remake is normally $40, but until November 17, Square Enix has made the digital versions of the Switch 2 ports available for $7.50 and $8, respectively. If you already own the series on PS5, Xbox Series X/S, or PC, it’s not worth picking up extra versions for the portability factor. There’s no nifty cross-save function like with Cyberpunk 2077. But for people who only have Switch 2s, these are easy pick-ups and will probably never be cheaper.

#3675. GTA 6 Preloading: Start Date And What To Know About Digital And Physical Copies

After years of development and multiple delays, Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto 6 is finally launching on November 19, and you can now actually preorder the game. The $80 game arrives on November 19, but you can actually preload it a week earlier, which is nice for the countless people who no doubt want to begin playing the second they can.

Here's everything you need to know about GTA 6 preloading.

GTA 6 preload schedule

GTA 6 players who preorder a digital copy of GTA 6 can begin preloading on Tuesday, November 10 at midnight local time in your respective time zone. This is to "ensure they are able to play at launch," Rockstar said, adding that code-in-box versions for both PS5 and Xbox Series X|S consoles should be available from retailers starting November 12.

The game's physical edition will be available to buy on November 12 "to support preloading," Rockstar said. So if you walk into a GameStop or Walmart on November 12 and see a copy of GTA 6 on the shelves to buy, you can do so, but the game itself won't unlock until November 19.

GTA 6 file size

GTA 6 is going to be massive, as Rockstar has confirmed the game will require up to 212GB of storage capacity, depending on your device.

GTA 6 launch times

GTA 6 launches on November 19, but when exactly? We don't know yet, as Rockstar has not yet shared that information. Keep checking back with GameSpot for the latest on GTA 6's launch times and more.

#3674. Melanie Lynskey Addresses ‘Insane’ Rumor About Her 'Two and a Half Men' Salary

Melanie Lynskey has opened up about what she earned while starring in Two and a Half Men.

“Sorry, but this insane number is floating around on the internet and I must tell you how wrong it is,” Lynskey, 49, who played Rose on the CBS sitcom, commented in response to an Instagram user’s October 25 claim that she made “$200,000 to $300,000” per episode.

She then detailed precisely what she received after appearing in 63 episodes out of the show’s total of 262. “I made literally one tenth of that stated number per episode. Started at $20,000 with I believe a 5 percent raise each season, but more than half of the episodes I did were in the first two seasons,” Lynskey continued. “The highest paycheck I got on the show was, I think, $43,000 for one episode in the final season.”

The Yellowjackets actress then added that large portions of her pay were then sliced up to remunerate other entities. “This is before agents, managers, business managers’ cuts, and taxes, so you take home around 50 percent of what you are paid,” she wrote, adding that her pay cheque suited her fine at the time. (Two and a Half Men ran for 12 seasons between 2003 and 2015.)

“I was extremely grateful for the job and for the money,” she explained. “It allowed me to pay my small mortgage, and pay bills, and be able to work in indie movies and build a career. But there is this insane idea that I made millions of dollars and it’s so ridiculous.”

The Instagram post that attracted Lynskey’s comments was originally shared by the “Alchemy With Anthony Mason” podcast and featured an interview with her Two and a Half Men costar Holland Taylor. In the interview, Taylor, 83, said that the show never paid her “very well” despite receiving four Emmy nominations. “They never gave me a raise,” Taylor said.

The social media user who claimed that Lynskey earned upwards of $200,000 also claimed that Taylor was paid “$75,000 an episode,” although no specific figures were mentioned by Taylor herself. The open conversation, however, motivated Lynskey to jump in with her own two cents.

“If Holland’s talking about it I’ll talk about it too 😂,” Lynskey concluded her comment.

She added another comment that went into further detail as to where she stood in life when she was part of Two and a Half Men. “I will say that that money was huge for me!! I was 25 years old when I got that job, and a couple of years in, I was able to put a down payment on a house,” Lynskey wrote. “I always think in terms of how lucky I am compared to the vast majority of actors because it is so, so hard to make a living. I had struggled so much at that point so I was very grateful. It wasn’t my show and I felt fine with what I was paid. I just get annoyed when it’s misreported.”

She added, “Also, Holland is, and was, a legend, and a queen, and deserved many raises!!!!”

#3673. One Popular PC Game Storefront Has Had Enough Of AI Slop, And It’s Taking Action

Indie game storefront Itch.io has announced it removed "a couple terabytes of AI slop" and has begun taking steps to combat the deluge of AI-created games appearing on the platform. "Just because you can upload 10 terabytes of poorly optimized AI-generated models doesn't mean you should upload 10 terabytes of poorly optimized AI-generated models," Itch wrote in a social media post.

The platform had already noted that the number of game pages being created per day had doubled from 3,000 to 6,000 over the last two months, with reports of users flooding the game uploads page with dozens of AI-created game spams. Going forward, Itch says that these sorts of bulk uploads will result in that spam being de-indexed, and filtering for generative AI disclosure will be added more sections of the site, including the search results page.

This doesn't mean Itch is outright banning AI-generated content, but it is taking a harder line against people who spam the site with it. In its official terms and conditions, Itch states that if the use of AI in a game is "clearly stated" and if "it adds substantial value" to the user experience, then that's okay. But if you're uploading something iterative, that'll be against the platform's rules.

Essentially, if you don't want to see AI-built games when you search Itch, the new filter will keep them out of your search results. This is a far stronger response than Valve's, as Steam's approach to AI slop has been very hands-off so far. While Valve has vaguely suggested it's considering how to address the influx of AI spam following the disastrous October edition of Next Fest, its response to developers fearful of AI-cloned projects has left much to be desired.

According to several developers, AI slop is a much bigger problem than Steam realizes.

Valve said that developers should focus on building a community and more unique features into their games to help stand out, which does nothing to address the issue of their projects being cloned the second they share progress online--although one of the big drivers behind cloned games, Anthropic's Claude, may have had its copycat abilities throttled recently.

#3672. Devs Are Blaming A Flood Of AI Slop On Steam For Delaying Their Games

November is, to put it lightly, nuts for video games. World of Warcraft: Forever launches tomorrow. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time will be out just a few hours after that. And a short two weeks after that, the juggernaut arrives: GTA 6. So as you might imagine, dozens of indie games are trying to get their releases out now, before these heavy hitters show up and suck all the air out of the room, monopolizing the time of content creators and players who might otherwise pay attention to smaller projects. But the folks behind a lot of those indie games are now worried they might be forced to launch right in the middle of that AAA maelstrom, thanks to what they believe to be a major bottleneck going on internally at Valve; one they think is caused by a flood of AI slop games.

Throughout October, multiple indies have posted on social media suggesting that their approvals process on Steam was taking longer than usual. Normally, Valve says it expects a 3-5 day waiting period when a developer submits a game for approval to appear on the Steam store. Valve then might get back to the developer with any issues it has, and it’s another few days to review again. Once Valve considers any such issues resolved, the game can then be published on the storefront. For all this, Valve specifically advises developers, “you’ll want to submit your page for review at least 7 business days before you want it live to account for potential changes you’ll need to make.”

Except recently, seven business days hasn’t cut it. Throughout October, a number of indie developers have posted on social platforms sharing that their reviews are taking two or three weeks or more to complete for no discernible reason.

There’s Caravarn Carnage: Fruity Road, for instance, which finally made it through Steam approvals on November 1 after submitting on October 16:

Hi @Steamworks, my games build has been stuck in review since October 16, beyond the usual 3-5 business days. I've contacted support but haven't received an update on the build review.

Ashen Legacy submitted on October 15, and was finally approved on November 1, coming in hot ahead of a planned November 6 release date:

Oh my god! My first submission was rejected, and Iâve already had to wait over two weeks. The scariest thing right now isnât the threat of AI-generated game clonesâitâs the wait for Steamâs review process. Itâs a race to see whose game gets approved first, and with my scheduledâ¦ pic.twitter.com/rgbgwK8PVE

— Ashen Legacy | Wishlist on Steam (@VerStudiovn) October 31, 2026

Lacey’s Flash Games was recently forced into a delay; it finally came out on Halloween, four days late:

And Wheel Make It was forced to launch three weeks late:

Wheel Make It has been unintentionally delayed while we're waiting on @Steam's approval.

The game was submitted for review 2 weeks ago, and was rejected because they couldn't figure out how to access local co-op (you literally just share a keyboard…)

The re-review has beenâ¦ pic.twitter.com/jLvB6QHZvK

— 2 Left Thumbs (@2_left_thumbs) October 12, 2026

Here’s a statement from Mira, one of the developers of the similarly-in-limbo Cubic Earth, provided to Kotaku:

We’re a small team, and we’ve spent a long time building up to getting our debut Early Access title, Cubic Earth, out into the world. Having it derailed last minute has been incredibly disheartening. Despite our best effort to follow Valve’s established processes and adherence to their stated timelines, our game now has no known launch window.

We’ve received a number of player complaints and questions across the Steam Community and YouTube, wondering why the game did not launch at the stated time. To make matters worse, organic traffic to our store page from Steam features has dropped off completely, and what was shaping up to be a promising Early Access launch now feels more like an anxiety inducing nightmare.

We’re hoping that this can be resolved as painlessly as possible, and trying to keep our eyes on the future!

Earlier today, I spoke at length to another impacted developer: Alfred Kamon, director of Studio Daimon, which is making Food Devils. Food Devils was supposed to launch today. It won’t be doing that, though, because it’s still awaiting Steam approval after being submitted way back on October 12.

Kamon says he first started to wonder if something was wrong about a week after the submission, with Valve still silent. On October 24, he followed Steam’s published advice for what to do if response was too slow: he submitted a support ticket. On the 26th, Valve responded with a concern about sexual content in the game, to which Kamon immediately replied in an attempt to resolve the issue. Now, seven days after that, he’s still waiting for a reply. Valve also responded to his support ticket, essentially telling him to wait for the review team to get back to him. (Kotaku has seen all of these messages between Kamon and Valve).

Kamon tells me that from his perspective, Studio Daimon did everything right in order to launch on time. Even with Valve having an issue with content, he says that in the past such problems have only taken 2-3 days to resolve, and he had prepared for that. He had not prepared for three weeks of waiting…and counting. He can’t even provide full game keys to reviewers until approvals are done (beta keys can and have gone out).

“Just before the release, everyone is crunching a lot just to finish everything, to do QA, to polish and to prepare all the content,” he said. “So everyone in the team maybe even stayed up late or even during weekends. It was very, very hard. And despite everything, I think it’s sad because everyone made so many sacrifices to be here now today, and we still couldn’t make it.”

What’s really ironic is that Food Devils‘ original release date was actually supposed to be November 5, but 24 hours before the team planned to announce it, Ocarina of Time planted its flag that same day. So the team moved it up. “Oh, no, we are not releasing on the same day as Zelda,” Kamon said. Of course, now there’s a solid chance they might.

I asked Kamon if it made sense to hold the game even longer, maybe into early December. After all, following Ocarina of Time is GTA 6. It’s a terrible month to release a small indie game, and Food Devils was originally getting in just barely under the wire. But Kamon tells me that’s not an option.

Studio Daimon is a small studio: just nine people, based in Italy, working on Food Devils for the last four years. It’s made one other game before, Path of the Midnight Sun, and it’s not exactly rolling in cash. Kamon tells me that the studio really needs the money from sales of Food Devils before the end of the year, and Steam pays out on a one-month delay. If Food Devils can’t launch soon, the studio might be in trouble financially.

Why is all this happening? We reached out to the company for comment and were directed to a blog post from today about the situation. In it, Valve acknowledges that it has seen “a significant increase in submissions for store page and build review in recent months,” noting later that the process is taking “up to 12 business days.” It goes on to say that most of that time is spent re-reviewing games that have issues at submission, and that in addition to adjusting its internal processes to help match the heavier load, Valve is also adding a number of items to its release checklist for developers that it says will help cut down on the number of submissions it needs to send back for adjustments.

What the blog post doesn’t mention is the role of generative AI, which many developers are theorizing is playing an outsized role in the massive wave of submissions. As of mid-October, more games have been released on Steam in 2026 than in all of 2025, with two and a half months to go. And in October alone, around 4,000 games were released on the platform, with nearly 50 percent of them disclosing some use of generative AI in development. That’s a lot of games coming through very, very fast, the speed aided by the ability of generative AI to churn out game-shaped things quickly. Developers suspect that, given these numbers, Valve is struggling to keep up with the sudden influx of submissions, and smaller studios without the clout to ask Valve to expedite their games are suffering for it. But without more specific word from Valve, no one can prove that’s what’s really happening.

The thing is, ValveÂ hasÂ acknowledged that the platform has some issue with AI slop. It finally made a statement last week, after over 8,000 demos flooded Steam Next Fest last month, alongside a report that a developer was extorted by someone threatening to make an AI clone of their project, as well as several developers admitting publicly that they hesitated to release game demos for fear of having their games cloned. But that statement was just that people at Valve didn’t want to be “gatekeepers telling developers which tools they should or shouldn’t use.”

Valve’s Marc Wilkinson also said, “We are fully aware of the situation, and a significant number of people are thinking about how to solve this problem.” But as much as one might appreciate how difficult it may be to figure out how to regulate AI, at the moment, a number of developers are actively suffering with no clear path to relief.

At this point, all Kamon wants is for Food Devils to be approved as soon as possible. He did say it would be nice to get some increased visibility on Steam to make up for this situation, since his release plans have now been all messed up through no fault of his own. And he wishes Valve would be transparent about how long the review process will take.

“I can also sympathize with those who have to review all these games,” he says. “But as a dev, at least I would like some honesty in the UI when you submit a game. Tell us it may take weeks. Just don’t promise us three to five days because then we make plans around the release date. We create hype. We announce everything. People are happy that the game is releasing and in the end, it doesn’t.”

#3671. I’m A Parks And Rec Fan, But I’d Never Heard Amy Poehler’s Sweet Take On What Leslie Knope Taught Her

Parks and Recreation has been off the air for over ten years, but I still find myself coming back to the workplace sitcom whenever I need to improve my mood. Pawnee feels like home; the characters always make me laugh, the heartwarming moments always make me cry, and I feel like I walk away from every rewatch having been taught a new life lesson.

Tom and Donna’s “Treat yo self” mantra, Leslie’s endless optimism, and Ron’s quiet way of loving and supporting those around him are just a few of the life lessons I’ve learned as a fan. As fans, we’re always more susceptible to latching on to characters and learning lessons because of how many times we’ll rewatch something; but stars themselves can also learn something from their time on a show. Case in point: Amy Poehler recently opened up about what playing one of the most beloved television characters of all time taught her.

Leslie Knope taught me a lot. Playing her really did improve my life. It made me a much better listener and more engaged person in the world. And it was really nice to come to work and, like, spend the whole day telling everybody how much you love them. I had to have a lot of energy to play her. And she gave me a lot of energy when I played her.

Parks and Rec was full of hilarious characters with big hearts, but it was Leslie who centered them all. Sure, sometimes she tried too hard and failed, but she always did things because she thought it would make a difference for the people of Pawnee. She’s definitely the reason why I always come back to the show and consider it one of the best sitcoms of all time.

To me, Poehler and Knope are basically the same person. Anyone who has ever listened to the Saturday Night Live alum speak over the years can attest to the way she seems to embody the Pawnee native. I’d never considered that she wasn’t always that way, but in listening to her mock job interview for WSJ Magazine, that wasn’t always the case.

That’s not to say Poehler was some terrible person pre-Parks and Recreation; anyone who worked with her on SNL would vouch for her kindheartedness — especially Andy Samberg, who credits Poehler with him pursuing Brooklyn Nine-Nine. There’s no denying she’s become an even better person because of Leslie. As she went on to say:;

So what I like about her and what I try to remember, and why I think I deserve this job, she never thought it was lame to care about things. So when I catch myself not caring about things, I do think about her. Because she wouldn't have that.

Not being afraid to care deeply about things is definitely the biggest message I’ve taken away from watching Parks and Rec, and it’s nice to hear the same is true for Poehler. She’s definitely taken that to heart in how she carries herself on her podcast and even with her charity endeavors, like back in 2020 when the Parks and Rec cast reunited to benefit Feeding America.

#3670. GTA 6 Worldwide Release Times Revealed, And The US Gets It Almost Last

GTA 6 is one of the most-anticipated games ever, and it arrives on November 19. People naturally want to know when exactly that day it will be available to play, and now Rockstar has confirmed the details.

The game will launch at midnight local time on November 19 "in all regions" across PS5 and Xbox Series X|S. Given that, it seems the US will be among the last major markets to get it.

The regional release rollout means people in New Zealand and Australia will get in first and the US will be among the final major regions to get started.

In short, GTA 6 will become available to play in New Zealand at midnight in the country, which works out to 5 AM PT / 8 AM ET on November 18. People in the US will then have to wait 16 hours to play GTA 6 where they live.

Given this, people in the US will be in for a tough day as they see the game go live for other people and have to wait. If you're concerned about spoilers, that's another reason to be on guard that day.

While GTA 6 unlocks on November 19, preloading for the 212GB game begins on November 10 for digital copies and November 12 for the code-in-a-box versions sold at retailers.

According to SensorTower, GTA 6 has already sold close to 7 million copies via preorders, and that number could climb to 25 million by launch. That would work out to more than $2 billion in revenue, which is reportedly enough to pay for the game's development budget.
